## INTRODUCTION:

By providing transcriptome-wide expression profiles for individual cells, single-cell genomic methods such as a single-cell or single-nucleus RNA sequencing have proven transformative to our understanding of the cellular diversity that underpins tissue behaviors in health or disease (Baysoy et al., 2023; Kolodziejczyk et al., 2015; Regev et al., 2017). With the ability to statistically define cell types and states and catalog cellular diversity in a wide range of tissues, these methods have empowered cellular atlasing efforts that are substantially extending our understanding of a wide variety of tissues in a broad range of organisms (Baysoy et al., 2023; Kolodziejczyk et al., 2015; Regev et al., 2017). However, these methods require the dissociation of cells from tissues and the extraction of RNAs from these cells prior to quantification; thus, an understanding of the organization of cells within tissues or of RNAs within cells is lost. Unfortunately, a wide variety of biological questions require an understanding of both transcriptome-scale gene expression and this essential spatial context.

Image-based approaches to single-cell transcriptomics, by contrast, quantify gene expression within individual cells within their native tissue context by directly imaging and identifying individual RNAs (Moffitt et al., 2022; Rao et al., 2021; Zhuang, 2021). As a result, they naturally provide both a measure of the organization of cells within a tissue and of RNAs within individual cells. Notable image-based methods include techniques such as in situ sequencing [ISS (Ke et al., 2013)], fluorescence in situ sequencing [FISSEQ (Lee et al., 2015)], sequential fluorescence in situ hybridization [seqFISH (Lubeck et al., 2014)], multiplexed error robust fluorescence in situ hybridization (MERFISH) (Chen et al., 2015), or spatially resolved transcript amplicon readout mapping [STARmap (Wang et al., 2018)]. However, the field is rapidly growing and new methods are being introduced rapidly (Liu et al., 2024). At their core, each of these methods identifies individual RNAs by generating fluorescent signals from individual molecules and discriminating unique RNA molecules by generating patterns of on-off fluorescence across multiple rounds of imaging—patterns that can be thought of as optical barcodes. Here we focus on MERFISH (Chen et al., 2015; Moffitt et al., 2018; Moffitt, Hao, Bambah-Mukku, et al., 2016; Moffitt, Hao, Wang, et al., 2016; Moffitt & Zhuang, 2016), which has emerged as a widely adopted method both academically and commercially, because of its combination of resolution, sensitivity, multiplexing, and high imaging throughput.

MERFISH generates fluorescent signals from individual RNA molecules using protocols inspired by single-molecule fluorescence in situ hybridization (smFISH), in which multiple short fluorescently labeled DNA oligonucleotides are bound to different regions of an mRNA of interest to produce bright fluorescent spots (Femino et al., 1998; Raj et al., 2008). In MERFISH, this process is modified. Multiple short DNA oligonucleotide probes, called encoding probes, are bound to target RNAs via a region of complementarity to those targets. These encoding probes also contain additional sequences, called readout sequences. In subsequent rounds of hybridization, distinct sets of readout probes—each complementary to a different readout sequence—are used to determine which readout sequences are contained on the encoding probes for each RNA. Unlike conventional smFISH methods in which a handful of different mRNAs are detected in one round of smFISH staining, MERFISH distinguishes hundreds to tens of thousands of unique RNA species by performing iterative rounds of FISH staining on the same sample, with different subsets of the targeted RNAs fluorescing in each smFISH image. The specific combination of readout sequences contained within the encoding probes directed to each RNA determines this pattern of fluorescence. This pattern can, in turn, be conceptualized as a binary barcode, with each smFISH image and, thus, readout sequence associated with each bit in the barcode. Critically, by leveraging error robust or correcting binary barcoding schemes, MERFISH can accommodate rare but consequential errors in smFISH measurements and perform high fidelity RNA identification in targeted measurements ranging from hundreds to over ten thousand (Chen et al., 2015; Moffitt et al., 2018; Moffitt, Hao, Bambah-Mukku, et al., 2016; Moffitt, Hao, Wang, et al., 2016; Moffitt & Zhuang, 2016; Xia et al., 2019).

Since its inception, MERFISH and its protocols have been primarily developed and applied for brain research. For instance, MERFISH has been used to identify and map neurons in specific brain regions (Allen et al., 2023; Fang et al., 2022; Moffitt et al., 2018; Osterhout et al., 2022; Sun et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2021) as well as in in large-scale tissue atlas projects that mapped the entire mouse brain (Yao et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2023). These measurements have identified and discovered a massive diversity of neuronal and non-neuronal types, mapped these cells in space, and, in many instances, have linked specific neuronal types to specific circuit functions (Allen et al., 2023; Fang et al., 2022; Moffitt et al., 2018; Osterhout et al., 2022; Sun et al., 2024; Yao et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2021, 2023). Collectively, these measurements underscore the discovery potential that image-based transcriptomics offers for a wide range of tissues. However, we have found that the protocols developed for the brain do not perform equally well in other tissues. One example is the gastrointestinal tract, where the use of the protocols developed for the brain can lead to RNA degradation and poor smFISH and MERFISH measurements.

Here we present a set of protocols and tips for performing MERFISH in the gastrointestinal tract. While these protocols draw on innovations such as hydrogel-based clearing methods (Moffitt, Hao, Bambah-Mukku, et al., 2016), or increased imaging throughput (Moffitt, Hao, Wang, et al., 2016) initially deployed in brain tissue and cell culture, the protocols presented here have been modified to address specific challenges, such as elevated RNase levels in the gut (Sun et al., 2024). These adaptations ensure high RNA integrity, preserve cell morphology, and maintain compatibility with immunofluorescence in the gut, crucial for accurately delineating cell boundaries and assigning detected RNAs to individual cells. We anticipate that these protocols may prove useful in other tissues as well.

Specifically, we provide a step-by-step guide on how to harvest and prepare mouse intestinal samples using either a fixed frozen (Basic Protocol 1) or a fresh frozen approach (Basic Protocol 2). We described how both protocols can be combined with immunofluorescence to target a pan-cell-surface marker (Alternate Protocol 1 and 2). This step is particularly important for cell segmentation and the accurate assignment of identified RNAs to individual cells. Moreover, we provide a description of alternative strategies for the digestion of lipids and proteins which helps clear the sample and reduce cellular autofluorescent background (Alternate Protocol 3). In the subsequent sections, we offer detailed instructions and tips on performing a MERFISH measurement, including how to amplify the encoding probe library targeting the genes of interest (Basic Protocol 3), to prepare the coverslips (Support Protocols 1 and 2), and to perform and analyze a MERFISH measurement (Basic Protocol 4 and 5) with imaging buffer preparation and microscope configuration (Support Protocols 3–5). The aim of these protocols is to provide laboratories interested in performing their own MERFISH measurements in the gut with the necessary expertise. More broadly, we also provide the rationale behind our protocol choices, along with tips and pitfalls, which should aid other laboratories in the adoption or modification of these protocols for other tissues. To aid in the use of these protocols, we explicitly reproduce common steps in many of these protocols.

CAUTION: Any step involving paraformaldehyde (PFA), formamide, hydrochloric acid, methanol, chloroform, allyltrichlorosilane, or triethylamine should be performed in a chemical fume hood.

CAUTION: It is essential that all tools (e.g., pipette, tips, etc.), laboratory benches and buffers are RNase free. Use a dedicated bench for RNA work and clean all equipment with solutions such as RNase Away or RNase Zap following the manufacturer’s instructions. The bench space and equipment should be cleaned daily.

CAUTION: Protocols involving animals must be reviewed and approved by the appropriate Animal Care and Ethical Committee.

## STRATEGIC PLANNING

The MERFISH sample preparation pipeline, from tissue harvesting to imaging and decoding, consists of a series of distinct protocol steps. The chronological workflow detailed in Figure 1 along with the expected execution time (detailed in the Time Consideration section) are aimed at assisting scientists in planning their experiments.

### Basic protocol 1

#### Protocol title: Fixed-frozen sample preparation

This protocol provides a comprehensive guide, covering all steps—from intestinal tissue harvesting to cryosectioning and mRNA library staining—necessary for conducting highly multiplexed RNA detection using MERFISH in fixed-frozen intestinal tissue, as described previously (Cadinu et al., 2024). Specifically, we begin by describing the harvesting of intestinal tissue, followed by fixation and cryoembedding. Next, we outline the process of cryosectioning and transferring the tissue onto pre-treated coverslips. This process is then followed by sample permeabilization and the first of two hybridization steps, where the poly-A tails of all RNA molecules are hybridized with anchoring probes. In the following step, the sample is embedded in a polyacrylamide hydrogel, and the probes are covalently bound to the gel. After this, lipids and proteins are digested in a clearing step that reduces non-specific binding of probes and improves the penetration of encoding probes in the next step. These encoding probes are longer than the anchoring probes (e.g. 95 nucleotides) and have limited penetration in fixed tissue, but their penetration improves after digestion. The second hybridization with a pool of encoding probes targeting the desired RNAs is then performed. Finally, the sample is washed and prepared for imaging.

#### Tissue harvesting and fixation

The purpose of this step is to rapidly harvest the intestine while preserving its cellular structure and RNA integrity through PFA fixation.

- In a 50 mL tube prepare fixation solution by adding the following: 4 mL 10x PBS.31 mL nuclease-free water.5 mL 32% PFA.

It is recommended to use a fresh ampule of PFA as the effectiveness of PFA can degrade with time, even when frozen.

- Chill the solution to 4°C.

Throughout the entire fixation process, it is crucial to maintain the temperature of both the harvested tissue and the buffer in which they are immersed at 4°C. This is essential for minimizing enzymatic activity and, consequently, preventing RNA degradation. In the dissection room, this step is typically achieved by utilizing a polystyrene box filled with ice.

- Load the repeater pipette with 5 mL of fixative solution.

- Pour 50 mL of the cold fixative solution on a 150 mm Petri dish.

- Quickly harvest the intestine and move it to the 150 mm Petri dish.

Iťs important to use separate tools for cutting the abdomen and the intestine to minimize RNase contamination, particularly from the skin. Wetting the skin with 70% ethanol before cutting the abdomen can minimize the risk of the skin and fur, which are rich in RNases, contacting the internal organs. RNA quality remains preserved when the animal is euthanized using either carbon dioxide or isoflurane.

It is important to note that this protocol is designed for both the small and large intestine. However, special care should be taken when dissecting the duodenum due to its connection to the pancreas. During dissection, pancreatic secretions—rich in RNases—may backflow into the duodenum. To minimize this risk, careful handling and avoiding unnecessary removal of pancreatic tissue are essential. Additionally, to prevent potential spillage, the duodenum can be backfilled with 1–2 mL of ice-cold fixative solution using a syringe fitted with a 27G needle right after opening the mouse abdomen and before removing the intestine.

- Connect one end of the harvested intestine to the repeater and flush with fixative solution to clear out the fecal content. 1 – 2 mL is generally sufficient.

You can attach a 200 μL pipette tip to the repeater pipette, which is thinner and better suited to the diameter of the mouse intestine. To minimize the risk of splashes, the intestine can be flushed inside a 50 mL conical tube after engaging the repeater.

- Transfer harvested tissue promptly to the ice-cold fixative solution in the conical tube and incubate for at least 3 hours at 4°C in a rocker.

Harvesting is a time-sensitive step. It is crucial to minimize the duration of tissue exposure to room temperature without fixative to preserve optimal RNA integrity. In general, the fixation time can be adjusted based on the specific tissue's thickness and density, which, in turn, influences PFA penetration and fixation rate. To ensure optimal results, the intestine should be harvested within 2–3 minutes, excluding the time for euthanasia.

- As the fixation is underway, prepare the dehydration solution. In a 50 mL tube add the following: 6 g sucrose.15.5 mL nuclease-free water.2 mL 10x PBS.

- Vortex until the sucrose is fully dissolved.

- Add 2.5 mL of 32% PFA to the dehydration solution above.

- Chill the solution at 4°C.

- After completing the fixation, gently transfer the tissue from the fixation solution to the dehydration solution using a pair of tweezers. Incubate overnight at 4°C.

It is essential that the sucrose is RNase and DNase free. The addition of PFA to the sucrose dehydration solution is optional but is routinely added to eliminate any residual RNase activity or RNase contamination from sucrose. We do not see adverse effects of the increased fixation due to adding PFA to this step.

- Incubate tissue in the sucrose-PFA solution overnight at 4°C.

#### Cryoembedding

The goal of this step is to carefully embed the tissue into cryoblocks, allowing both long-term storage at −80°C and cryosectioning.

- Fill the cryomold with OCT and chill to 4°C.

Cryoembedding is performed in the cold room at 4 °C. Avoid any bubbles in the OCT, as they can pose challenges during cryosectioning. If there are bubbles, restart by filling a fresh cryomold with OCT.

- Transfer the tissue along with the dehydration solution onto a large Petri dish.

- Using scissors and tweezers, carefully cut the intestine (small or large intestine) along its longitudinal axis into pieces measuring approximately 3 to 4 mm.

The dimensions strictly depend on the size of the cryomold. However, in the case of the intestine, extremely long pieces are not recommended as they are harder to be filled with OCT in the next step.

- Transfer the pieces onto a cryomold and make sure they are completely covered with OCT (Figure 2).

One or multiple pieces can be placed in the same cryomold (Figure 2, A–B). Tweezers can be used to gently orient the intestine so that the cross section is parallel to the surface. Care should be taken that the intestinal fragments are completely filled with OCT as bubbles will introduce challenges when cryosectioning.

- Freeze the cryomold by putting it into contact with dry ice (Figure 2, C).

Note that during this step, the color of OCT changes from transparent to white matte when fully frozen. An alternative freezing approach involves using a mixture of 100% ethanol and dry ice. In this case, using tweezers, gently lower cryomolds into contact with the ethanol-dry-ice bath but be careful to avoid submerging the block completely into this bath until the block is fully frozen.

- Transfer the cryoblocks into ziploc plastic bags and place at −80°C for long-term storage.

#### Cryosectioning

The purpose of this step is to produce 10-μm-thick tissue sections which are then placed onto coverslips.

- Prepare the cryostat: Pre-chill the cryostat to −20°C.Mount the blade and move all the required sectioning tools (e.g., brushes, tweezers) in the cryostat and allow them to equilibrate to the temperature of the cryostat.

- Using tweezers, transfer the PDL-coated coverslips (Supporting Protocol 2) into small Petri dishes. Move the Petri dishes into the cryostat and let them equilibrate to the temperature of the cryostat for ~1 hour.

- Using a bucket filled with dry ice, transfer the cryoblock from the −80°C freezer into the cryostat chamber and let it equilibrate to the temperature of the cryostat for about 1 hour.

- Remove the tissue block from the cryomold and mount on the sample holder. Place a small amount of OCT at the base of the sample holder.Before the OCT freezes, place the tissue block onto it.Use the heat extractor inside the cryostat, typically a metal cylinder, to secure the sample in place and allow the OCT to freeze for 5 minutes before proceeding.

This step can be redone if the block is not mounted properly.

- Move the sample holder to the sectioning platform and clamp it on the adjustable specimen head. Adjust the sample orientation with respect to the blade before moving forward.

- Bring the block closer to the blade by using the motorized stage mount and the handwheel. Ensure the desired section thickness is selected.

The optimal thickness is approximately 10 μm. Substantially thicker samples exceed the imaging depth of oil immersion objectives and increase the background fluorescence. Thinner samples have smaller cell volumes that are imaged and, thus, less total RNA counts per cell.

- Slice sections until the desired plane in the tissue is found.

It is recommended to discard the first few slices of tissue as they represent the edges of the samples and might have lower RNA quality. Additionally, you can use non-PDL-coated coverslips to spot-check the tissue architecture with a bright-field microscope.

- Once the desired depth is reached, place a PDL-coated coverslip on the sectioning platform. Slice a section of the tissue.

If the tissue is curling an excessive amount, letting the cryostat ‘rest’ or cool back down to −20 °C can be helpful. Fast slicing can warm up the blade and block and result in low quality slices.

- Use the tweezers to transfer the tissue slice to the center of the coverslip and melt it by gently touching the back of the coverslip with your gloved finger. Refreeze the coverslip by placing it in contact with any metal plate inside the cryostat.

- Inside the cryostat, use the tweezers to carefully move the coverslip into a small Petri dish.

Alternatively, one can gently touch the non-PDL-coated side of the coverslip with a gloved fingertip to warm it and then drop this coverslip gently onto the frozen slice to melt and adhere. Once the tissue is melted, the coverslip should be moved to a metal surface in the cryostat to rapidly refreeze it. The coverslip can then be returned to a Petri dish.

- Once all desired slices are collected, move the Petri dishes outside the cryostat onto the lab bench, remove the lid, and let the slices dry for 30 minutes at room temperature.

When completely dried, the tissue will be translucent and the OCT around the tissue will turn from a glossy to more matte appearance.

During this drying phase, the tissue gradually enhances its adherence to the PDL-coated coverslip. If this step is omitted, then the tissue will detach from the coverslip during subsequent preparation steps.

- Prepare a fixation solution by adding the following to a 50 mL tube: 4 mL 10x PBS.31 mL nuclease-free water.5 mL 32% PFA.

- Transfer the samples into the chemical hood.

- Using a pipette, gently transfer 1 mL of this fixation solution to each slice, such that the entire slice is covered. Incubate for 10 minutes at RT.Aspirate the fixation solution.

- Wash coverslips by decanting 3 mL of 1xPBS into each Petri dish. Incubate the sample in 1xPBS for 2 minutes.Aspirate the 1xPBS.Decant an additional 3 mL of 1xPBS into each Petri dish.Move immediately to the permeabilization step below.

#### Permeabilization

The purpose of this step is to permeabilize the membranes of fixed cells so that probes can penetrate.

- Prepare a solution of 70% ethanol in nuclease-free water by adding the following to a 50 mL tube: 35 mL 100% ethanol.15 mL nuclease-free water.

- Prechill to 4°C.

- Place each coverslip into a fresh 60-mm diameter Petri dish containing 3 mL 70% ethanol Use tweezers to delicately lift the coverslips and eliminate any solution trapped below it.Incubate for 45 seconds.

- Aspirate the 70% ethanol and add 4 mL of fresh 70% ethanol solution to each Petri dish.

- Seal the Petri dishes with parafilm to minimize evaporation.

- Store the samples at 4°C for at least 12 hours to permeabilize the samples.

Samples can be stored for at least a week at 4°C in the permeabilization solution. Thus, this point can be a convenient pause point in the protocol.

#### Pre-Hybridization Wash

This step aims at changing the buffer and preparing the samples for the upcoming hybridization.

- Prepare a pre-hybridization solution comprised of 30% formamide in 2x SSC. In a 50 mL tube mix the following: 5 mL 20x SSC.30 mL nuclease-free water.15 mL formamide.Gently invert the tube multiple times to mix the solution.

- Remove each sample from the 4°C storage above and aspirate the 70% ethanol.

- Add 3 mL of the pre-hybridization solution to each sample. Gently lift the coverslip using tweezers to remove any leftover solution underneath the coverslip.Incubate for 2 minutes.Repeat this wash for a total of two times.

Care should be taken to avoid mechanical stress to the tissue slice. Thus, solutions should be slowly poured or pipetted at the edge of the Petri dish.

#### Hybridization with anchoring probes

This step aims to hybridize all poly-adenylated RNAs by utilizing anchoring probes containing a poly-T sequence. If immunostaining is required (e.g., cell membrane staining to perform cell segmentation), refer to Alternate Protocol 2 for antibody preparation and staining.

- Prepare a hybridization chamber: Add a layer of parafilm to the bottom of a large Petri dish, and gently press down with a cap from a 50 mL tube to ensure the parafilm adheres to the surface.

- Prepare 50 μL of staining solution in hybridization buffer for each sample. This buffer should contain mRNA anchoring probes at a final concentration of 2 μM. For details on the preparation of hybridization buffer, please refer to the Supporting Protocol 3.

- To prepare the staining solution, first, add hybridization buffer to a 1.5 mL LoBind tube, then add the anchoring probes. Vortex vigorously for 30 seconds. Notably, the anchoring probe volume should never exceed 10% of the total staining solution volume (e.g., no more than 5 μL for a 50 μL staining solution). This limit prevents diluting the formamide concentration in the hybridization buffer which in turns impacts hybridization.

Adjust the volume of the hybridization solution according to the tissue area to be stained.

- Using tweezers, move the dish into the large Petri dish (the tissue is facing up).

- Aspirate the excess formamide from the sample before you pipette the hybridization mixture.

Notice that residual wash buffer will decrease the concentration of probes in the hybridization mixture; thus, care should be taken to minimize the amount of residual buffer. Blotting on a Kimwipe can also be helpful.

- Pipette 50 μL of hybridization mixture on top of the tissue slices so that it completely covers the tissue. Take care not to touch the tissue slice with the pipette tip or pipette directly on top of the tissue itself.

Depending on the tissue area, adjust the hybridization volume accordingly. On this step, it is important to move quickly to prevent the tissue from drying out.

- Repeat the hybridization step for all the remaining dishes.

- Wet a Kimwipe with nuclease-free water and place inside the hybridization chamber.

The Kimwipe will saturate the humidity inside the chamber and avoid evaporation of the hybridization solution.

- Place the Petri dish in a humidified 37°C hybridization oven and incubate for 48 hours.

A standard cell culture incubator can be used for the hybridization oven. If the incubator is also being used for cell culture, it is recommended to clean the outside of the large Petri dish with 70% ethanol before adding it to the incubator.

#### Post-Hybridization Wash

The aim of this step is to remove probes that are either unbound or non-specifically bound to the sample.

- In a chemical hood, prepare a post-hybridization wash buffer. In a 50 mL tube mix the following: 5 mL 20x SSC.30 mL nuclease-free water.15 mL formamide.Gently remove each coverslip from the parafilm and place in a small Petri dish with the tissue facing up.

To save plasticware, the Petri dishes could be the same used before the hybridization.

- Cover immediately with 3 mL of post-hybridization wash solution.

As above, to avoid mechanical damage to the tissue slice pour or pipette solutions gently on the edge of the Petri dish.

- Incubate for 30 minutes in a 47°C incubator located inside the chemical hood.

- Aspirate the wash solution and add 3 mL of fresh post-hybridization wash solution and incubate for 30 minutes in the 47°C incubator located inside the chemical hood.

- Aspirate the wash solution and add 3 mL of post-hybridization wash.

- Immediately proceed to “Embedding and Clearing”.

#### Embedding and Clearing

The embedding step serves to incorporate the sample in a polyacrylamide hydrogel, providing stable support for the mRNAs which are bound to the gel via the acrydite moiety present in the anchoring probes. The subsequent clearing step aims to reduce background fluorescent signal by degrading proteins with enzymatic treatment and removing lipids with detergent. The final step of the clearing procedure involves thoroughly washing the samples to remove the clearing agent (SDS), which is difficult to eliminate and can interfere with fluorescence imaging under the microscope.

#### Preparing Gel-Slick Coated Microscope Slides

The goal of this step is to apply a silane layer to the glass slide which prevents the polyacrylamide gel from adhering to them.

- Prepare gel-slick coated microscope slides as follows: Wash one microscope slide for each coverslip with RNase-zap and then 70% ethanol.Dry with a Kimwipe.Add 0.5 mL of GelSlick to the center of each microscope slide.Gently spread this solution to cover the entire slide with a Kimwipe.Incubate for 1 minute at RT.Remove this solution with a Kimwipe so that the surface is completely dry.

#### Embedding sample into a hydrogel

- In a 1.5 mL tube prepare a solution of 10% w/v ammonium persulfate in water by adding 100 mg of ammonium persulfate to 1 ml of nuclease-free water. Vortex for 20 seconds to fully dissolve.

This solution should be prepared fresh each time.

- In a 50 mL tube, mix the following: 3 mL 5 M NaCl.2.5 mL 1 M TrisHCl pH 8.5 mL 40% 19:1 acrylamide/bis-acrylamide solution.39.5 mL of nuclease-free water.

- Mix gently by inverting the tube 5 times.

- Add 75 μL of TEMED to the tube.

- Mix gently by inverting the tube 5 times.

- Add 150 μL of ammonium persulfate solution to the tube.

- Mix gently by inverting the tube 5 times and degas the solution in a vacuum chamber for 5 minutes.

The gel solution is polymerizing. Therefore, move quickly through the next steps.

- Aspirate 2xSSC from each Petri dish containing a coverslip.

- Add 3 mL of degassed embedding solution to sample and incubate at RT for 2 min to allow the gel solution to penetrate the tissue slices. Gently lift the coverslip to remove any 2xSSC trapped below the coverslip.

- Aspirate gel solution from samples.

- Again, add 3 mL of gel embedding solution to each Petri dish.

Do not aspirate the excess gel solution from the coverslip. Keeping the coverslip covered with gel solution will prevent bubbles from being trapped when the coverslip is inverted onto the GelSlick-coated microscope slide.

- Pipette a 65 μL droplet of gel embedding solution to the center of a GelSlick-coated microscope slide (Figure 3, A).

- Using tweezers, gently remove the coverslip from the Petri dish, invert it, and slowly place it onto the droplet on the glass slide (Figure 3, B).

The tissue is facing the glass slide. Do this step gently, taking care not to trap air bubbles and avoiding sliding the dish onto the glass slide, as it can damage the tissue.

- Incubate at room temperature for 1.5–2 hours to allow gel to fully polymerize (Figure 3, C).

#### SDS-based digestion

- In a 50 mL tube prepare the digestion buffer by mixing the following: 3 mL 20xSSC.21 mL nuclease-free water.6 mL 10% SDS.0.3 mL 25% Triton-X solution.Mix gently by manually inverting the tube.0.3 mL Proteinase K.Mix gently by inverting the tube.

- Add 3 mL of digestion buffer onto a small Petri dish.

- With a razor blade and a tweezer, gently remove each coverslip from the glass slide. Place in the small Petri dish.

The gel and, thus, the sample should face up.

- Place in a 37°C humidified incubator overnight.

For difficult to clear tissues, this digestion can be repeated with a fresh digestion buffer and an additional day of incubation. As SDS can be difficult to remove from samples, an alternative digestion buffer can be used that is less effective at hard-to-clear samples but is rapidly and easily removed (see Alternate Protocol 3).

#### Wash Samples after SDS-based digestion

The aim of this step is thoroughly wash the samples to eliminate SDS which is challenging to remove and can interfere with fluorescent readout at the microscope.

- Use tweezers to transfer samples to the 3D printed storage container (Figure 4A).

- Fill the container with 2xSSC and use parafilm to cover the top and avoid any dust or particles coming into contact with the sample (Figures 4B & C).

- Rock gently for 30 minutes at RT.

- Repeat this wash a total of 6 times and then place the samples in fresh Petri dishes in 2x SCC.

Since SDS is difficult to remove from the samples, it is important to perform at least six washes. Residual SDS can create fluorescent background in samples in the form of bright and often large spots. If such features are observed, increase the number of washes for subsequent samples. Washed samples can be stored in Petri dishes covered with 2XSSC at 4°C for at least a week.

#### Pre-Hybridization wash

This step aims at changing the buffer and preparing the samples for the upcoming hybridization.

- Prepare a pre-hybridization solution comprised of 30% formamide in 2x SSC. In a 50 mL tube mix the following: 5 mL 20X SSC.30 mL nuclease-free water.15 mL formamide.

- Aspirate the 2XSSC from each sample.

- Add 3 mL of hybridization wash mixture to each sample. Gently lift the coverslip using the tweezer.

#### Hybridization with encoding probes

In this step, the goal is to facilitate the hybridization of encoding probes with the targeted RNAs.

- Prepare a hybridization chamber: Add a layer of parafilm to the bottom of a large Petri dish and gently press down with a cap from a 50 mL tube to ensure the parafilm adheres to the surface.

Each large Petri dish can fit up to 4 coverslips.

- Prepare 50 μL of encoding staining solutions per sample in the hybridization buffer (refer to Support Protocol 3 for hybridization buffer recipe). Vortex vigorously for 30s.

The concentration of the encoding library depends on the specific library used, as it is a function of the number of oligos in the library. It is recommended to conduct a titration experiment to evaluate the optimal library concentration that maximizes the signal-to-noise ratio of single molecule FISH (smFISH), and thus, the overall RNA detection efficiency. In general, low library concentrations give rise to dim smFISH spots and low detection efficiency. Similarly, staining samples with an excessively high concentration might lead to high fluorescent background, low smFISH signal-to-noise ratio, and modest detection efficiency. For instance, for a library targeting ~1000 genes, which consists of about 70,000 oligos, reasonable concentrations may range between 30 μM and 50 μM.

Notably, the encoding probe volume should never exceed 10% of the total staining solution volume (e.g., no more than 5 μL for a 50 μL staining solution). This limit prevents diluting the formamide concentration in the hybridization buffer which in turn may impact the oligo hybridization.

- To minimize the dilution of the hybridization solution, trim the gel as following: Remove the coverslip from the Petri dish and place it on top of a Kimwipe to remove excess solution (Figure 5A).Using a razor blade, trim the gel around the sample (Figure 5B).By using the hydrophobic pen, mark the region around the trimmed gel (Figure 5C).

The hydrophobic boundaries ensure that the hybridization solution does not spread outside the gel.

- Place the coverslip inside the large Petri dish with the hydrogel facing up.

- Add one droplet of 50 μL of hybridization mixture on top of the gel (Figure 5D).

It is recommended to adjust the hybridization mixture volume according to the gel size (typical range is 50 μL to 100 μL). Before adding the hybridization solution, it is recommended to minimize the pre-hybridization left on top of the gel as this can dilute the hybridization mixture. Excess solution can be sucked via capillary force by gently applying a Kimwipe at one corner of the gel or by using the tip of a vacuum aspirator in proximity to the corner of the gel.

- Insert a wet Kimwipe in a corner of the hybridization chamber.

This represents an extra precaution as the incubator oven is already humidified.

- Place the hybridization chamber at 37°C in a humidified oven and incubate for at least 48h.

It is important to place the dishes on a level area of the oven, as a slight tilt in the samples can lead to accumulation of hybridization solution on one side of the sample.

The incubation time varies with library size and, thus, can be extended. In general, the larger the library, the longer the incubation time required for the probes to diffuse and bind to their target inside the gel. If the hybridization oven is humidified, the only disadvantage to increasing the duration of the hybridization is the increase in the overall protocol duration. It is recommended to run a titration experiment where samples of the same batch are incubated for different times (e.g., 2 days, 3 days, and 4 days) to determine the optimal time.

#### Post-Hybridization wash and storage

The aim of this step is to remove encoding probes that are either unbound or loosely bound to the sample and to store the sample before imaging.

- Prepare a post-hybridization wash buffer. In a 50 mL tube mix the following: 5 mL 20x SSC.30 mL nuclease-free water.15 mL formamide.

- Gently remove each coverslip from the parafilm and place in a 60-mm diameter Petri dish. Petri dishes could be the same used before the hybridization.Make sure that the tissue slices are always facing up.

- Cover immediately with 3 mL of post-hybridization wash solution.

- Place the dishes in a 47°C oven for 30 minutes.

- Aspirate the hybridization wash solution and add 3 mL of fresh post-hybridization wash solution.

- Place the dishes in the 47°C oven which is inside a fume hood for 30 minutes.

- Aspirate the hybridization wash solution and add 3 mL of 2xSSC to cover each sample. Gently lift the coverslip.

- Aspirate the 2x SSC and add 5 mL fresh 2x SSC.

- Store the samples at 4°C in the fridge and image them with MERFISH within a week.

### Basic Protocol 2

#### Protocol title: Fresh-frozen sample preparation

This protocol provides a comprehensive guide, covering all steps—from intestinal tissue harvesting to cryosectioning, library staining, sample embedding, and clearing—necessary for conducting highly multiplexed RNA detection using MERFISH in fresh-frozen intestinal tissue (Petukhov et al., 2022). While this protocol shares many steps with the fixed-frozen method, there are a few key differences worth noting. Fresh-frozen tissue does not suffer from the poor penetration of long probes that occurs with fixed tissue. Consequently, both the anchoring and encoding probes can be combined into a single hybridization step, which can also accommodate antibody staining if necessary. For simplicity for the reader, we, nonetheless, replicate the shared elements of the protocol in their entirety below.

#### Tissue harvesting and cryoembedding

This step aims to harvest the intestine, preserving its cellular structure and RNA integrity. The tissues are flushed with a preservation solution containing Ribonucleoside Vanadyl Complex (RVC), a small molecule RNAse inhibitor. The tissue is then carefully embedded into cryoblocks for long-term storage.

- Prepare the tissue preservation solution. In a 50 mL tube mix the following: 5 mL 10x PBS.44 mL nuclease-free water.1 mL 200 mM RVC.

The color of the preservation solution should be emerald green. Any deviation in color may signal solution degradation. Note that the stock RVC aliquots must be preheated prior to use. We recommend following the manufacturer’s instructions for this step and then aliquoting single-use aliquots that are stored at −20°C.

- Chill the solution at 4°C.

- Load the repeater pipette with 5 mL of preservation solution.

- Pour 50 mL of the preservation solution (4 mM RVC in 1x PBS) on a large Petri dish.

- Quickly harvest the tissue and move it to the large Petri dish.

Iťs important to use separate tools for cutting the abdomen and the intestine to minimize RNase contamination, particularly from the skin. Wetting the skin with 70% ethanol before cutting the abdomen can minimize the risk of the skin and fur, which are rich in RNases, contacting the internal organs. RNA quality remains preserved when the animal is euthanized using either carbon dioxide or isoflurane.

- Connect one end of the harvested intestine to the repeater and flush with preservation solution to clear out the fecal content. 1 – 2 mL is generally sufficient.

You can attach a 200 μL pipette tip to the repeater pipette, which is thinner and better suited to the diameter of the mouse intestine. To minimize the risk of splashes, the intestine can be flushed inside a 50 mL conical tube after engaging the repeater.

- Tissue is stable in the preservation solution for up to 1 h at 4°C.

In the harvesting process, preserving optimal RNA integrity critically depends on the harvesting time. Minimizing tissue exposure to room temperature is crucial as it reduces enzymatic activity and prevents RNA degradation. Adding RVC, which specifically inhibits RNase activity, provides an additional layer of protection for RNA. To ensure optimal results, the intestine should be harvested within 2–3 minutes, excluding the time for euthanasia.

- Fill the cryomold with OCT and chill to 4°C.

Cryoembedding is performed in the cold room at 4°C. Avoid any bubbles in the OCT, as they can pose challenges during cryosection. If there are bubbles, restart by filling a fresh cryomold with OCT.

- Transfer the tissue along with the preservation solution onto a large Petri dish.

- Using scissors and tweezers, carefully cut the intestine along its longitudinal axis into pieces measuring approximately 3 to 4 mm.

The dimensions strictly depend on the size of the cryomold however, in the case of the intestine, extremely long pieces are not recommended as they are harder to be filled with OCT in the next step. Note with this exact approach it is possible to prepare intestinal tissue in a Swiss roll fashion.

- Transfer the pieces onto a cryomold and make sure they are completely covered with OCT (Figure 2).

One or multiple pieces can be placed in the same cryomold (Figures 2A & B). Tweezers can be used to gently orient the intestine so that the cross section is parallel to the surface. Care should be taken that the intestinal fragments are completely filled with OCT as bubbles will introduce challenges when cryosectioning.

- Freeze the cryomold by putting it into contact with dry ice (Figure 2C).

Note that during this step, the color of OCT changes from transparent to white matte when fully frozen. An alternative freezing approach involves using a mixture of 100% ethanol and dry ice. In this case, using tweezers, gently lower cryomolds into contact with the ethanol-dry-ice bath but be careful to avoid submerging the block completely into this bath until the block is fully frozen.

- Transfer the cryoblocks into ziploc plastic bags and place at −80°C for storage.

#### Cryosectioning

The purpose of this step is to produce 10-μm-thick tissue sections which are then placed onto coverslips.

- Prepare the cryostat. Pre-chill the cryostat to −20°C.Mount the blade and move all the required sectioning tools (e.g. brushes, tweezers) in the cryostat and allow them to equilibrate to the temperature of the cryostat.

- Using tweezers, transfer the PDL-coated coverslips (Supporting Protocol 2) into small Petri dishes. Move the Petri dishes into the cryostat and let them equilibrate to the temperature of the cryostat for ~1 hour.

- Using a bucket filled with dry ice, transfer the cryoblock from the −80°C freezer into the cryostat chamber and let it equilibrate to the temperature of the cryostat for about 1 hour.

Note that large cryoblocks (e.g., 1 cm ×1cm × 4 mm) might require longer time to equilibrate.

- Remove the tissue block from cryomold and mount on the sample holder. Place a small amount of OCT at the base of the sample holder.Before the OCT freezes, place the tissue block onto it.Use the heat extractor inside the cryostat, typically a metal cylinder, to secure the sample in place and allow the OCT to freeze for 5 minutes before proceeding.

This step can be redone if the block is not mounted properly.

- Move the sample holder to the sectioning platform and clamp it on the adjustable specimen head. Adjust the sample orientation with respect to the blade before moving forward.

- Bring the block closer to the blade by using the motorized stage mount and the handwheel. Ensure the desired section thickness is selected.

The optimal thickness is approximately 10 μm. Substantially thicker samples exceed the imaging depth of oil immersion objectives and increase the background fluorescence. Thinner samples have smaller cell volumes that are imaged and, thus, less total RNA counts per cell.

- Slice sections until the desired place in the tissue is found.

It is recommended to discard the first few slices of tissue as they represent the edges of the samples and might have lower RNA quality. Additionally, you can use non-PDL-coated coverslips to spot-check the tissue architecture with a bright-field microscope.

- Once the desired depth is reached, place a PDL-coated coverslip on the sectioning platform. Slice a section of the tissue.

If the tissue is curling an excessive amount, letting the cryostat ‘rest’ or cool back down to −20°C can be helpful. Fast slicing can warm up the blade and block and result in low quality slices.

- Use the tweezers to transfer the tissue slice to the center of the coverslip and melt it by gently touching the back of the coverslip with your finger.

- Inside the cryostat, use the tweezers to carefully move the coverslip into a small Petri dish.

Alternatively, one can gently touch the non-PDL-coated side of the coverslip with a gloved fingertip to warm it and then drop this coverslip gently onto the frozen slice to melt and adhere. Once the tissue is melted, the coverslip should be moved to a metal surface in the cryostat to rapidly refreeze it. The coverslip can then be returned to a Petri dish.

- Using tweezers, carefully move the coverslip into a small Petri dish that has been equilibrated to −20 °C inside the cryostat chamber.

To enhance overall slice adherence, remove the lid from every Petri dish and allow the OCT to sublimate for approximately 2 hours at −20°C inside the cryostat.

- While the tissue is drying prepare the fixation solution by adding the following to a 50 mL tube: 4 mL 10x PBS.31 mL nuclease-free water.5 mL 32% PFA.Chill the solution to 4°C.

Once all sections are cut and dried inside the cryostat chamber for about 2 hours, move on to the fixation step.

- Utilize a closed lid foam box with dry ice on the bottom to transfer the dishes with the lids to a 4°C cold room or a bucket filled with ice-water slurry.

Iťs crucial to avoid melting the slices during transport.

- Gently pipette ~5 mL of cold fixation solution so that all slices are completely covered. Incubate for 20 minutes at 4°C.Aspirate the fixation solution.

- Wash coverslips by pouring 5 mL of 4°C 1xPBS and incubate for 5 min at 4°C. Aspirate the 1x PBS and pour fresh 5 mL 1x PBS at 4°C.

- Move immediately to the permeabilization step.

#### Permeabilization

The purpose of this step is to permeabilize the membranes of fixed cells so that MERFISH encoding probes can penetrate.

- Prepare a solution of 70% ethanol in nuclease-free water by adding the following to a 50 mL tube: 35 mL 100% ethanol.15 mL nuclease-free water.

- Pre-chill to 4°C.

- Place each coverslip into a fresh 60-mm diameter Petri dish containing 3 mL 70% ethanol. Use tweezers to delicately lift the coverslips and eliminate any solution trapped below it.Incubate briefly.

- After a brief incubation (less than 1 minute), aspirate the 70% ethanol and add 4 mL of fresh 70% ethanol solution to each Petri dish.

- Seal the Petri dishes with parafilm to minimize evaporation.

- Store the samples at 4°C for at least 12 hours to permeabilize the samples.

Samples can be stored for at least a week at 4°C in the permeabilization solution. Thus, this point can be a convenient pause point in the protocol.

#### Pre-Hybridization Wash

This step aims at changing the buffer and preparing the samples for the upcoming hybridization.

- Prepare a pre-hybridization solution comprised of 30% formamide in 2x SSC. In a 50 mL tube mix the following: 5 mL 20x SSC.30 mL nuclease-free water.15 mL formamide.Gently invert the tube multiple time to mix the solution.

- Remove each sample from the 4°C storage above and aspirate the 70% ethanol.

- Add 3 mL of the pre-hybridization solution to each sample. Gently lift the coverslip using tweezers to remove any leftover solution underneath the coverslip.Incubate for 2 minutes.Repeat this wash for a total of two times.

Care should be taken to avoid mechanical stress to the tissue slice. Thus, solutions should be slowly poured or pipetted at the edge of the Petri dish.

#### Hybridization with anchoring probes and encoding probes.

This step aims to hybridize all poly-adenylated RNAs by utilizing anchoring probes containing a poly-T sequence and encoding probes targeting selected RNAs. If immunostaining is required (e.g., cell membrane staining to perform cell segmentation), refer to the Alternate Protocol 1 for antibody preparation and staining.

- Prepare a hybridization chamber: Add a layer of parafilm to the bottom of a large Petri dish, and gently press down with a cap from a 50 mL tube to ensure the parafilm adheres to the surface.

- Prepare 50 μL of staining solution in hybridization buffer for each sample. This buffer should contain mRNA anchoring probes at a final concentration of 2 μM and encoding probes. For details on the preparation of hybridization buffer, please refer to Supporting Protocol 3. If your sample requires antibody staining, please refer to Alternate Protocol 1. To prepare the staining solution, first add hybridization buffer to a 1.5 mL tube. Then, add the anchoring probes and encoding probes. Vortex vigorously for 30 seconds. Notably, the anchoring and encoding probe volume should never exceed 10% of the total staining solution volume (e.g. no more than 5 μL for a 50 μL staining solution). This prevents diluting the formamide concentration in the hybridization buffer which in turn may impact oligo hybridization.

Adjust the volume of the hybridization solution according to the tissue area to be stained.

The concentration of the encoding library depends on the specific library used, as it is a function of the number of oligos in the library. It is recommended to conduct a titration experiment to evaluate the optimal library concentration that maximizes the signal-to-noise ratio of single molecule FISH (smFISH), and thus, the overall RNA detection efficiency. In general, low library concentrations give rise to dim smFISH spots and low detection efficiency. Similarly, staining samples with an excessive concentration might lead to high fluorescent background, low smFISH signal-to-noise ratio, and modest detection efficiency. For instance, for a 1000 genes library which consists of about 70000 oligos, reasonable concentrations may range between 30 μM and 50 μM.

Notably, the encoding probes volume should never exceed 10% of the total staining solution volume (e.g. no more than 5 μL for a 50 μL staining solution). This limit prevents diluting the formamide concentration in the hybridization buffer which in turns impacts on the oligo hybridization.

- Using tweezers, move the dish into the large Petri dish (the tissue is facing up).

- Aspirate the excess formamide from the sample using the aspirator before you pipette the hybridization mixture.

Notice that residual wash buffer will dilute the concentration of probes in the hybridization mixture; thus, care should be taken to minimize the amount of residual buffer.

- Pipette 50 μL of the hybridization mixture on top of the tissue slices so that it completely covers the tissue.

Depending on the tissue area, adjust the hybridization volume accordingly. On this step, it is important to move quickly to prevent the tissue from drying out.

- Repeat the hybridization step for all the remaining dishes.

- Place a Kimwipe wetted with nuclease-free water inside the hybridization chamber.

The Kimwipe will saturate the humidity inside the chamber and avoid evaporation of the hybridization solution.

- Place the Petri dish in a 37°C hybridization oven that is humidified and incubate for at least 48 hours. Make sure the outside of the Petri dish is clean by using 70% ethanol before placing it in the incubator.

The incubation time varies with library size and thus can be extended. In general, the larger the library, the longer the incubation time required for the probes to diffuse and bind to their target inside the gel. It is recommended to run an optimization experiment where samples of the same batch are incubated for different times (e.g., 2 days, 3 days, and 4 days) and RNA detection efficiency measured with MERFISH is compared.

#### Post-Hybridization Wash

The aim of this step is to remove probes that are either unbound or non-specifically attached to the sample.

- In a chemical hood, prepare a post-hybridization wash buffer. In a 50 mL tube mix the following: 5 mL 20x SSC.30 mL nuclease-free water.15 mL formamide.Gently remove each coverslip from the parafilm and place in a 60-mm diameter Petri dish.

Note that the Petri dishes could be the same as the ones used before the hybridization.

- Cover immediately with 3 mL of post-hybridization wash solution.

As above, to avoid mechanical damage to the tissue slice pour or pipette solutions gently on the edge of the Petri dish.

- Incubate for 30 minutes in a 47°C incubator located inside the chemical hood.

- Aspirate the wash solution and add 3 mL of fresh post-hybridization wash solution and incubate for 30 minutes in the 47°C incubator located inside the chemical hood.

- Aspirate the wash solution and add 3 mL of post-hybridization wash.

- Immediately proceed to “Embedding and Clearing”.

#### Embedding and Clearing

The embedding step serves to incorporate the sample in a polyacrylamide hydrogel, providing stable support for the mRNAs which are bound to the gel via the acrydite moiety present in the anchoring probes. The subsequent clearing step aims to reduce background fluorescent signal by degrading proteins with enzymatic treatment and removing lipids with detergent. The final step of the clearing procedure involves thoroughly washing the samples to remove the clearing agent (SDS), which is difficult to eliminate and can interfere with fluorescent imaging under the microscope.

#### Preparing Gel-Slick Coated Microscope Slides

The goal of this step is to apply a silane layer to the glass slide which prevents the polyacrylamide gel from adhering to them.

- Prepare gel-slick coated microscope slides as follows: Wash one microscope slide for each coverslip with RNase-zap and then 70% ethanol.Dry with a Kimwipe.Add 0.5 mL of GelSlick to the center of each microscope slide.Gently spread this solution to cover the entire slide with a Kimwipe.Incubate for 1 minute at RT.Remove this solution with a Kimwipe so that the surface is completely wet.

#### Embedding sample into a hydrogel

- In a 1.5 ml LoBind tube prepare a solution of 10% w/v ammonium persulfate in water by adding 100 mg of ammonium persulfate to 1 ml of nuclease-free water. Vortex for 20 seconds to fully dissolve.

This solution should be prepared fresh each time.

- In a 50 mL tube, mix the following: 3 mL 5 M NaCl.2.5 mL 1 M TrisHCl.5 mL 40% acrylamide/bis-acrylamide solution.39.5 mL of nuclease-free water.

- Mix gently by inverting the tube 5 times.

- 75 μL TEMED.

- Mix gently by inverting the tube 5 times.

- 150 μL of ammonium persulfate solution to the tube.

- Mix gently by inverting the tube 5 times and degas the solution in a vacuum chamber for 5 minutes.

The gel solution is polymerizing. Therefore, move quickly through the next steps.

- Aspirate 2xSSC from each Petri dish containing a coverslip.

- Add 3 mL of degassed embedding solution to sample and incubate at RT for 2 min to allow the gel solution to penetrate the tissue slices. Gently lift the coverslip to remove any 2XSSC trapped below the coverslip.

- Aspirate gel solution from samples.

- Again, add 3 mL of gel embedding solution to each Petri dish.

Do not aspirate the excess gel solution from the coverslip. Keeping the coverslip covered with gel solution will prevent bubbles from being trapped when the coverslip is inverted onto the GelSlick-coated microscope slide.

- Pipette a 65 μL droplet of gel embedding solution to the center of a GelSlick-coated microscope slide (Figure 3A).

- Using tweezers, gently remove the coverslip from the Petri dish, invert it, and slowly place it onto the droplet on the glass slide (Figure 3B).

The tissue is facing the glass slide. Do this step gently, taking care not to trap air bubbles and avoiding sliding the dish onto the glass slide, as it can damage the tissue.

- Incubate at room temperature for 1.5–2 hours to allow gel to fully polymerize (Figure 3C).

#### SDS-based digestion

- In a 50 mL tube prepare the digestion buffer by mixing the following: 3 mL 20xSSC.21 mL nuclease-free water.6 mL 10% SDS.0.3 mL 25% Triton-X solution.Mix gently by manually inverting the tube.0.3 mL Proteinase K.Mix gently by inverting the tube.

- Add 3 mL of digestion buffer onto a small Petri dish.

- With a razor blade and a tweezer, gently remove each coverslip from the glass slide. Place in the small Petri dish.

The gel and thus the sample should face up.

- Place in a 37°C humidified incubator overnight.

For difficult to clear tissues, this digestion can be repeated with a fresh digestion buffer and an additional day of incubation. As SDS can be difficult to remove from samples, an alternative digestion buffer can be used that is less effective at hard-to-clear samples but is rapidly and easily removed (see Alternate Protocol 3).

#### Wash Samples after SDS-based digestion

The aim of this step is to thoroughly wash the samples to eliminate SDS which is challenging to remove and can interfere with fluorescent readout at the microscope.

- Use tweezers to transfer sample to the 3D printed storage container (Figure 4).

- Fill the container with 2xSSC and use parafilm to cover the top and avoid any dust or particles coming into contact with the sample (Figure 4).

- Rock gently for 30 minutes at RT.

- Repeat this wash a total of 6 times and then place the samples in fresh Petri dishes in 2x SCC.

Since SDS is difficult to remove from the samples, it is important to perform at least six washes. Washed samples can be stored in Petri dishes covered with 2x SSC at 4°C for a week prior to MERFISH imaging.
