#### Protocol steps with step annotations:

#### Purification binding beads buffer

This protocol aims to prepare a bead-based purification solution suitable for purifying large amounts of RNA or DNA material obtained from in vitro transcription and reverse transcription reactions.

To prepare the DNA binding beads, the following supporting buffers are required:

- 10% Tween20 In a 50mL tube mix the following: 5 mL of Tween 20.45 mL of nuclease-free water.Mix solution on a rotary mixer for at least one hour to fully dissolve.Store at room temperature.

- PEG 8000 stock solution. In a 50 mL tube mix the following: 20 g of PEG 8000.11.2 mL of nuclease-free water.Place the tube in a hotplate at 60°C until the powder is completely dissolved.

It may be necessary to rock the solution overnight to fully dissolve the PEG powder.

- Store at room temperature

- Bead Wash Buffer. In a 50 mL tube, mix the following: 48.75 mL nuclease free water.1 mL TE Buffer.250 μL 10% Tween 20.Store at room temperature.

- Bead Salt Buffer. In a 50 mL tube, mix the following: 3.75 mL nuclease-free water.25 mL 5M NaCl.1 mL TE pH 8.Vortex to mix.Store at room temperature

- Label an empty 50 mL tube as “DNA binding beads buffer.”

- Vortex vigorously the Sera-Mag bead bottle to ensure the beads are re-suspended.

- Immediately transfer 1 mL of beads to a 1.5 mL LoBind tube.

Move quickly in this step as the beads settle rapidly.

- Place the tube on a magnet and allow the beads to separate. Remove the supernatant.Add 1 mL of Bead Wash Buffer.Remove the tube from the magnet and vortex for at least 15s.Gently spin down to bring excess liquid to the bottom of the tube.Put the tube back on the magnet and allow beads to separate.

- Repeat the steps in 8 twice for a total of 3 washes.

- Remove the supernatant.

- Add 1 mL of the Bead Salt Buffer from above.

- Remove the bead tube from the magnet and vortex well for 15s.

- Spin down at 100 × g for 30 seconds to avoid pelleting the beads.

- To the 50 mL tube (“DNA binding beads buffer”), add the following: 28.75 mL Bead Salt Buffer.1 mL of the beads from above.Vortex to mix.20 mL PEG 8000 Stock Buffer.

Dispense slowly as the liquid is viscous.

- 250 μL 10% Tween 20.

- Mix very gently by inverting the tube many times.

- Store at 4°C

The volume of purification binding beads generated is ample for purifying more reactions than needed for a single run of the encoding probe construction protocol.

#### In vitro Template Production

The aim of this step of the protocol is to amplify a template for in vitro transcription from the complex oligopool template library. Limited cycle PCR is used to prevent the formation of chimeric molecules and to limit amplification bias. The following steps are written for 40 reactions as an example. However, they can be scaled up or down to match the desired final yield.

#### Primer and Library Dilutions

- Make a 5 μM-each working mix of the forward and reverse primer in nuclease-free water.

- Make a 1/400 dilution of the complex oligopool (library).

Typical oligopool dilutions range from 1/100 – 1/1000 and depend on the amount of amplifiable material provided in the complex oligopool. As this value is not determined by the amount of starting material, as the starting material contains variable amount of non-amplifiable truncated molecules, it is best set by running an initial small scale limited-cycle PCR. We select a dilution such that the cycle at which the sample is amplified to half of the maximum fluorescence is between 15 and 18.

#### Limited-Cycle PCR

It is critical to stop this amplification before the amplification reaches the final plateau which normally occurs between 15 and 25 cycles. As primers and other reagents are exhausted late in the amplification, we find that appreciable amounts of cross-priming between template oligos can occur, leading to the creation of chimeric molecules.

- Per reaction, mix the following: 500 μL nuclease-free water.200 μL 1/400 diluted library.100 μL 20x EvaGreen.200 μL of 5 μM each of the forward and reverse primer.1000 μL 2X Phusion Hot Start Master Mix.

- Mix with a 1 mL pipette set to 900 μL by pipetting up and down 25 times.

- Dispense 50 μL to wells in a 96-well PCR plate. Seal the plate with the appropriate film.

A few reactions (~3) can be dispensed into a second plate, which will be run first to determine the proper number of cycles at which to run the first plate (Figure 6A). Plates can be stored after preparation in a 4°C fridge if not being used immediately.

- Run the following program on a qPCR machine: 98°C ramp up, 2 minutes.98°C melt, 10 seconds.56°C anneal, 15 seconds.72°C extend, 20 seconds.Measure fluorescence in each well.72°C extend, 5 seconds (This extra step allows one to pause at 72°C after the measurement).Repeat the melting, annealing, extension, and measurement steps until the rate of the sample amplification reaches the inflection point and then stop the amplification (Figure 6B).

Adjust the annealing temperature according to the oligos used by using the temperature suggested by the New England Biolabs’ melting temperature online tool (https://tmcalculator.neb.com/).

#### DNA Purification

The aim of this step is to purify the in vitro templates produced via qPCR following the Zymo DNA Clean and Concentrator protocol.

- To a 15 mL tube add the following: Add 12 mL of Zymo DNA binding buffer (a 6:1 ratio of DNA binding buffer to sample is needed).Add 2 mL of qPCR run above.Mix via vortex.

- Bind DNA to Zymo columns. Place 3 Zymo Spin III columns in collection tubes.Add ~700 μL of this mixture to each spin tube and spin in a tabletop centrifuge at 10,000 × g for 30 s.Discard flow through.Repeat with the same spin columns until all the DNA solution has been passed across a column.

This process can also be run on a vacuum manifold to reduce the number of spin steps.

- Wash each column with 400 μL of DNA wash buffer and spin at max (at least >10000 × g) speed for 30 seconds.

- Discard flow through and repeat this wash once more.

- Carefully take out columns and place into 1.5 mL LoBind tubes

- Add 200 μL nuclease-free water to each column. Incubate for 2 minutes.

This incubation step increases the recovery yield by favoring the return to solution of nucleic acids captured in the column.

- Spin at 13,000 × g for 30 seconds.

- Pool eluted DNA into one 1.5 LoBind tube.

- Remove 20 μL of DNA and store in a 0.5 mL tube for quality control purposes. Use 2 μL to measure the concentration and spectrum with the UV-Vis spectrophotometer.

The total volume recovered should be about ~600 μL. Typical concentrations are ~10–20 ng/μL. However, these concentrations can vary substantially given the cycle at which the limited-cycle PCR is stopped. Note that the in vitro transcription is designed to saturate and, thus, can tolerate variation in the input template concentration. A concentration less than 5 ng/μL, however, is indicative of a failure in the reaction.

#### In vitro transcription

The purpose of this part of the protocol is to generate RNA from the DNA template amplified from the above qPCR. This protocol is a modified version of that provided with the NEB HiScribe kit.

- In each of three 1.5 mL LoBind tube, mix the following: 190 μL template DNA (from above).175 μL nuclease-free water.30 μL 100 mM CTP.30 μL 100 mM GTP.250 μL NTP Buffer mix (this is part of the HiScribe kit).Mix well via vortex, then add the following:25 μL Murine RNase Inhibitor.50 μL T7 polymerase mix.

Note that extra GTP and CTP are added to improve the efficient amplification of templates that contain our readout sequences (which use a reduced nucleotide alphabet). Work with tubes and reagents in an ice-water slurry to keep all reagents cold prior to running the reaction.

- With a 1000 μL pipette set to 500 μL, pipette up and down 25 times to mix the sample.

- Incubate the reaction at 37°C in a humidified incubator for at least 12 hours.

To avoid external contamination, the tubes are placed in a secondary container such as a clean 50 mL tube or a plastic bag.

#### RNA Purification via beads

The aim of this step is to both purify and concentrate the RNA generated via the in vitro transcription.

- In six 2 mL LoBind tubes, mix the following: 375 μL of in vitro transcription.1125 μL of purification beads.Manually invert the tubes to mix the solution.

The volume ratio between purification beads and in vitro transcription should be 3:1.

Ensure that the purification beads are at room temperature. If they were stored at 4°C, allow them sufficient time to reach room temperature before use.

- Incubate for 15 minutes at room temperature.

- While the mixture is incubating prepare 70% ethanol solution. In a 50 mL tube add the following: 35 mL 100% ethanol.15 mL nuclease-free water.Invert the tube multiple times.

This solution must be prepared fresh from ice cold 100% ethanol.

- Use the minicentrifuge to quickly spin down the tubes.

A few seconds are enough to bring excess fluid on the side of the tubes down to the bottom.

- Place the tubes on the Dynamag magnet and allow the beads to separate out of solution (Figure 7A).

The time to separate can vary depending on magnet strength. Typically, 25 minutes is sufficient for a full separation. If the solution appears cloudy, increase the incubation time.

- Keeping the tubes on the magnet, carefully remove and discard the supernatant without disturbing beads.

This is done by using a 1000 μL pipette.

- Add 800 μL 70% ethanol to the tubes still on the magnet.

Adjust the volume as needed to completely cover beads.

- Incubate for 2 minutes.

- With the beads still on the magnet, remove and discard supernatant carefully.

- Repeat the 70% ethanol wash one more time.

- Remove excess ethanol from the bottom of the tube.

- Open the tubes while on the magnets and allow the ethanol to evaporate at room temperature (Figure 7B).

Beads should not be overdried. At the beginning of the process beads appear translucent. In contrast when the beads are fully dry, they will appear dark brown and matte. When beads are overdried, they will be light brown in color and the bead pellet will show extensive cracks. Overdried beads can lead to low RNA recovery.

- Add 100 μL of nuclease-free water to each of the tubes and resuspend the beads by gently pipetting.

Take care to wash the pellet completely from the side of the tube.

- Briefly spin the tubes in a mini centrifuge to bring excess liquid to the bottom of the tube. Alternatively, you may use a tabletop centrifuge and spin the tubes at 2,000 × g for 10 seconds.

- Place the tube back on the magnet to separate the beads from the solution.

It typically takes approximately 10–15 minutes for the beads to fully separate.

- Transfer eluent into a fresh tube.

- Combine samples in a single tube.

- Remove about 30 μL of RNA and store it at −20°C in a new 0.5 mL LoBind tube for quality control purposes. Measure the concentration as well as the spectra with the spectrophotometer.

The typical reaction will yield ~100–200 μg of RNA per 30 μL of the original in vitro transcription reaction. The RNA can be stored at −20°C or −80°C before being used for the next steps of the protocol which is the reverse transcription.

#### Reverse Transcription

The aim of this step of the protocol is to generate DNA encoding probes from the RNA template.

- Fill a 1 L beaker with 1 L of nuclease-free water and place it inside the 50°C incubator. Set the incubator temperature to 50°C.

Run this step a day in advance so that the water temperature has time to rise to 50°C.

- In a 1.5 mL LoBind tube, prepare the 25 mM dNTP mix by mixing the following: 250 μL of 100 mM dATP.250 μL of 100 mM dTTP.250 μL of 100 mM dCTP.250 μL of 100 mM dGCP.Vortex thoroughly.

- Store at −20°C.

Avoid multiple freeze-thaw cycles for dNTP mix, so aliquot into single use aliquots after creating this mixture. It is recommended to thaw dNTPs and Maxima buffer on ice as they are unstable at room temperature.

- On ice, in a 5 mL LoBind tube, prepare the reverse transcription mixture by adding: XX μL of purified RNA from in vitro.

Depending on the yield (concentration and volume of the in vitro reaction), adjust the XX volume so that the final RNA concentration is 3–4 μg/μL which corresponds to 150 μg – 200 μg or RNA per reaction. Loading more than 200 μg of RNA per reaction does not increase the overall yield of the RT reaction.

- YY μL of nuclease-free water.

Adjust the water volume YY so that the total reaction volume including all of the following components is 3600 μL.

- 720 μL of 5x RT buffer.

- 432 μL of 25 mM dNTP mix.

- 432 μL of RT Forward Primer.

The RT forward primer stock concentration is 400 μM and its final concentration is 48 μM.

- 50 μL of RNasin.

- 50 μL of Maxima H-RT.

Gently pipette the solution before and after adding the enzymes RNasin and Maxima to ensure the solution is fully mixed.

Note that increasing the Maxima H-RT concentration can lead to a modest increase in the overall yield at the expense of the cost per reaction. Similarly, reducing the amount of input RNA can increase the fraction of RNA converted to DNA, albeit at the cost of the total amount of DNA produced in each reaction volume.

- Aliquot the reaction above into 0.5 mL volumes in 2 mL LoBind tubes.

- Incubate for 1.5 hours in the 50°C incubator.

Leverage a plastic floater or any other plastic holder to place the tubes in the water bath.

- Proceed immediately to the alkaline hydrolysis.

#### Alkaline Hydrolysis

The aim of this step is to break down the RNA template and (optional) cleave off the reverse transcription primer from the probes.

- In a 10 mL tube mix the following: 4 mL of 0.5 M EDTA.4 mL 1 N NaOH.Vortex to mix well.

- Remove the tube from the incubator and add an equal volume (e.g., 500 μL in this case) of the mixture above to each 2 mL tube containing the reverse transcription.

- Incubate at 95°C for 15 minutes in the 95°C hot plate.

- Add 250 μL 1 N HCl to each 2 mL tube. Mix well.

- Move immediately to the purification step.

Measure pH by transferring small amounts of the reaction to pH paper and adjust to pH 7 using 1 N NaOH or 1 N HCl as needed.

#### Probe Purification

The aim of this step is to both purify and concentrate the final probe.

- In a 50 mL tube, combine the following: 9 mL of alkaline hydrolysis reaction.27 mL of purification beads.Mix well via vortex.

- Split equally the volume into two 50 mL tubes.

- Place the tube on the 3D custom built magnet rack and allow the beads to separate out of solution (Figure 8A).

Reducing the total volume will speed up the drying process later in the protocol.

Wait until the solution is clear which might take approximately 30 minutes. Note that the duration could vary depending on scale (Figure 8B). All beads should be clustered near the magnet. If the solution is still cloudy, increase the incubation time until the solution is completely clear. Proceeding before the solution is clear will result in the loss of some beads and a decrease in the recovery.

- While the mixture is incubating on the magnet, prepare 70% ethanol solution. In a 50 mL tube add the following: 35 mL 100% ethanol.15 mL nuclease-free water.Invert the tube multiple times.

Must be prepared fresh from ice-cold 100% ethanol.

- After the beads have separated from the solution, collect and discard the supernatant without disturbing beads.

- Add 20 mL 70% ethanol to the tube.

- Vortex vigorously.

Make sure to fully dislodge and resuspend the beads.

- Place the tubes back into the magnets and incubate for about 2 minutes.

This incubation is fast because ethanol is not as viscous as the purification beads solution. Nevertheless, wait until the beads are fully clustered against the magnets and the solution is clear.

- Remove supernatant carefully.

- Again add 15–20 mL 70% ethanol to the tube still on the magnet.

- Incubate for 2 minutes.

- Remove as much ethanol as possible.

- Open the tubes while on the magnets and allow the ethanol to evaporate at room temperature (Figure 8C).

As above, it is critical to not over dry beads.

- Add 400 μL of nuclease-free water into each tube.

Be careful to fully dislodge and resuspend the pellet. Failure to do so will result in low DNA yield.

- Transfer to a fresh 1.5 mL LoBind tube.

- Incubate at room temperature for 15 minutes.

- Place the tube back on the smaller magnet to separate the beads from the solution. Typically, 10–15 minutes.

- Transfer eluent into a fresh LoBind tube.

- Place the tube on the magnet to separate any beads that were carried over.

- Incubate for a few minutes to allow beads to separate.

- Transfer eluent into another fresh tube. Use 2 μL to measure the concentration and spectrum with the UV-Vis spectrophotometer

- Aliquot into single-use aliquots and store at −20°C.

A typical reaction yields ~25–100 μM final concentration of encoding probes. If a higher concentration is needed, then move to the Concentration of encoding probes via ethanol precipitation step below.

#### Concentration of encoding probes via ethanol precipitation

This optional concentration step is useful if the final concentration of probes used for staining is greater than 10 μM.

- In a 2 mL LoBind tube add the following: 1 volume of the DNA library made above.1/10 volume of 3 M sodium acetate (pH 5.5).3 volumes of 100% ice cold ethanol.Vortex to mix.

- Spin down at maximum speed (>13000 × g) for 30 min at 4°C.

It is possible to centrifuge at room temperature; however, the yield will decrease.

- Gently pipette off the supernatant, without disturbing the pellet at the bottom of the tube.

- Add 400 μL of ice-cold 70% ethanol.

- Spin down at maximum speed (>13000 × g) for 5 min.

- Remove as much ethanol as possible.

- Open the lid and allow the content to dry at room temperature.

When the DNA is fully dry it is possible to see the translucent pellet at the bottom of the tube.

- Add nuclease-free water.

Adjust the elution volume to achieve a final concentration of approximately 400–500 μM.

- Vortex vigorously to resuspend the DNA in solution and quickly spin down the tube.

- Repeat this step twice.

- Measure the concentration and spectrum with the UV-Vis spectrophotometer.

- Aliquot and store at −20°C.

As an alternative to ethanol precipitation, the library can be concentrated by evaporating the solution in a vacuum chamber at RT (typically overnight or longer) and then resuspending it in the desired volume.

#### Quality Control

The purpose of the quality control is to use a denaturing gel to assay the quality of the probes and different intermediate products generated in the protocol above.

#### Casting an 8% denaturing polyacrylamide gel

- In a 0.5 mL beaker, mix the following: 24 g of urea.15 mL of nuclease-free water.5 mL 10x TBE.10 mL 40% 19:1 acrylamide/bis-acrylamide.

- Cover with parafilm, and mix and heat on a hotplate at no more than 50°C until fully dissolved

- In a 1.5 mL LoBind tube prepare a 10% ammonium persulfate (APS) solution by mixing the following: 100 mg of APS.1 mL of nuclease-free water.

- Set up casting apparatus frames with appropriately sized short plates and glass plates.

- Once the gel solution has reached room temperature, add 75 μL of TEMED and mix the solution.

- Then add 150 μL of 10% APS and mix briefly.

- Pour the gel solution quickly into the plates before the gel begins to crosslink.

- Insert the appropriately sized comb.

- Let the gel crosslink for about an hour.

Denaturing gels can be stored in a plastic bag at room-temperature for ~1 week.

#### Running the gel

- Prerun the gel for 30 minutes at ~110 V in 1x TBE.

- Prepare the samples for loading by mixing 10 μL of Urea Loading Buffer and 10 μL of samples.

Samples to be run are the purified DNA template generated with the qPCR, RNA generated via in vitro transcription, and DNA generated via the reverse transcription.

- Prepare 2 μL of Generuler Ultra Low Range Ladder (or similar ladder), 8 μL of water or TBE, and 10 μL of Urea Loading Buffer.

- Load 10 μL of the ladder mix and sample mixes into the lanes of the gel.

It is recommended to titrate the DNA generated via the reverse transcription. Higher concentration might better illustrate the presence of small unwanted products.

- Run the gel at 120 V for 30 minutes at 60°C (in water bath if possible). Heating the gel during running helps maintain denaturing conditions.

- Dissemble the gel apparatus and stain for 30 minutes using 1x GelGreen in 1X TBE.

- Wash briefly in 1X TBE.

- Image the gel (Figure 9).

As the in vitro transcription removes the reverse primer and the T7 promoter (which sometimes are the same sequence), the RNA should be shorter than the DNA. If a reverse transcription primer contains a 3’ RNA nucleobase, then the alkaline hydrolysis will remove the forward primer, and the final template DNA should be shorter than the RNA.

We observe a small degree of ‘smearing’, i.e. shorter products, in the final encoding probe solution. If no probe is produced or this ‘smear’ is far more abundant than the band of expected length, it is possible that there is RNase contamination in the reverse transcription reaction. We recommend doing a small test run without Maxima enzyme, purifying this reaction prior to alkaline hydrolysis, and running on the gel to test for such contamination.

### Basic Protocol 4

#### Protocol title: MERFISH imaging

This protocol details the preparation of imaging buffers necessary for a complete MERFISH acquisition, including the volumes and the order in which they are flowed during the process.

#### Materials

20x Saline Sodium Citrate [SSC] (Invitrogen, AM9763)

PCA - 3,4-Dihydroxybenzoic acid (VWR, AC11489–0250)

Trolox - 6-hydroxy-2,5,7,8-tetramethylchroman-2-carboxylic acid (Sigma, 238813–5G)

NaOH (Sigma, 72068–100ML)

rPCO - Bacterial Protocatechuate 3,4-Dioxygenase (OYC Americas, 46852004)

Methanol (Sigma, MX0480–1)

Ethylene carbonate (Sigma, E26258–500G)

Triton X-100 (Sigma, T8787–50ML)

Trolox-Quinone (see Supporting Protocol 4)

0.5 M TCEP (see Supporting Protocol 5)

RNase/DNase-free nuclease-free Water

Light mineral oil (Sigma, M5904-6×500ML)

Vacuum chamber (VWR, 54929-051)

24-well plate (Thomas Scientific, 1162B94)

3D printed buffer holder (https://github.com/MoffittLab/3DParts)

50 mL tubes (Corning, 430828)

Rotating mixer

Balance

Aspirator

#### Protocol steps with step annotations:

#### Prepare the imaging buffers

The purpose of this step is to prepare the imaging, cleavage, wash and SSC buffers required to perform a full MERFISH acquisition.

#### 2X SSC buffer

This buffer is designed to wash away the cleavage buffer before initiating another hybridization round.

- To a 50 mL tube add the following: 5 mL 20x SSC.45 mL of nuclease-free water.

#### Cleavage buffer

The reducing agent in this buffer is used to cleave the disulfide bond that binds the fluorophore to the readout probe.

- To a 50 mL tube add the following: 4.5 mL 20X SSC.4 mL of 0.5 M TCEP aliquot.36.5 mL of nuclease-free water.

TCEP aliquots are stored in the −20°C and quickly thawed in a hot plate at 60°C.

#### Wash buffer

This buffer serves a dual purpose. First, it washes the sample after the post-hybridization wash. Second, it is utilized during the hybridization of the readout probes. The primary component, ethylene carbonate, is used to lower the nucleic acid melting temperature, disrupting secondary structures. We use ethylene carbonate as opposed to formamide, as it is considered non-toxic. This process facilitates the hybridization of readout probes and favors their removal when loosely bound to off-targets.

- In a 50 mL tube prepare 50% ethylene carbonate solution by adding the following: 15 mL of nuclease-free water.15 mL of ethylene carbonate.

Ethylene carbonate solid can be melted in either a water bath or a hot plate at 60°C and then aliquoted out and stored at RT in the dark prior to use.

- In a 50 mL tube prepare 25% Triton X-100 solution by mixing the following: 10.7 g of Triton X-100.29.3 mL of nuclease-free water.Mix the solution in a rotary mixer overnight at RT.

This can be stored at RT indefinitely.

- In each of three 50 mL tubes prepare the wash solution by adding the following: 5 mL 20x SSC.10 mL 50% ethylene carbonate.0.2 mL 25% Triton X.

- Fill to 50 mL with nuclease-free.

If necessary, use the hot plate at 60°C to re-melt the ethylene carbonate aliquot. Depending on the samples to stain and the number of bits of the library you may need more or less wash buffer.

#### Imaging buffer

The combination of an oxygen scavenger system (rPCO and its substrate PCA) and a redox pair, serving as triplet-state quenchers (Trolox-Trolox Quinone), enhances the brightness and stability of fluorophores.

- In a 1.5 mL LoBind tube prepare 100mg/mL Trolox by adding the following: 100 mg Trolox.1 mL methanol.Vortex thoroughly.

- In a 1.5 mL LoBind tube prepare 2.5 M PCA by adding the following: 386 mg PCA.1 mL methanol.Vortex thoroughly.

Both PCA and Trolox solution can be stored at −20 °C between use for up to two weeks. If Trolox or PCA precipitate out, do not use.

- In a 50 mL tube prepare the imaging buffer by adding the following: 4 mL of Trolox-Quinone.36 mL 2x SSC.80 μL 2.5 M PCA.200 μL 100 mg Trolox.200 μL 1 M NaOH.

- Load the imaging buffer, wash buffer, cleavage buffer and 2x SSC into the 3D printed cartridge holder and degas all the solutions in vacuum chamber for at least 10 minutes.

Loosen the cap before engaging the vacuum.

- Add 80 μL of rPCO enzyme to the imaging buffer and gently invert the tubes 3 times to mix the solution.

Minimize buffer oxygenation by restricting its exposure to open air and swiftly loading it onto the fluidic system, following the described procedure.

#### Readout probe cartridge

The readout probe cartridge holds the fluorophore coupled oligonucleotide sequences (readout) solutions utilized throughout a complete MERFISH run, enabling the sequential rounds of hybridization.

- Thaw the readout probes needed for experiment.

- Add 5 mL of wash buffer prepared above with a serological pipet to the needed wells of plate.

For instance, for a dual-color experiment with 16-bit library, only wells 2 to 8 require wash buffer (readouts corresponding to bit 1 and bit 2 are stained at the bench).

- Fill the unused wells with 5 mL of nuclease-free water.

- Use a multi-channel pipet add 15 μL of readout probe aliquot to the corresponding wells so that the final concentration is 3 nM.

Limit the exposure of the cartridge to ambient light and dust.

#### On-bench sample staining

The objective of this step is to stain the sample with the initial sets of readout probes (e.g., readout probes associated with bit 1 and bit 2) and, if desired, a nuclear marker.

- In a 15 mL tube, mix the following: 3 mL of the wash buffer prepared above.9 μL of 1 μM stocks of the desired readout probes.Vortex to mix.

- Aspirate 2x SSC buffer from the sample of interest in a 60-mm diameter Petri dish.

- Cover the sample with ~3 mL of the hybridization mix.

- Cover with foil and gently rock for 15 minutes at room temperature.

- In a separate 15 mL tube, mix the following: 3 mL of the ethylene carbonate hybridization buffer.12 μL of 1 mg/mL DAPI.Vortex for 5 seconds.

- Aspirate samples.

- Cover with this additional wash/DAPI-stain solution.

- Cover with foil and gently rock for 2 minutes at room temperature.

- Aspirate solution from the samples.

- Cover with 2x SSC.

- Samples can be stored briefly before being imaged.

#### Microscope pre-imaging

The purpose of this step is to prime the fluidic system by flushing all the tubing with their respective buffer.

- Turn on the MERFISH setup and confirm all hardware including the fluidic system, the light engine, autofocus system, cameras and stage is on and working properly.

- Adjust illumination based on the brightness of the smFISH spots, co-staining, and the camera settings. See Table 1 for typical values.

It’s important to note that variation in the illumination region will require proportional scaling of the power.

- Load both the readout cartridge and the cartridge holding the SSC, wash, cleavage, and imaging buffers.

- Add 3–4 mL of mineral oil to the imaging and cleavage buffer to minimize the air exposure which might lead to premature buffer degradation.

Imaging and cleavage buffers are sensitive to oxygen. Excessive exposure to oxygen results in premature buffer aging, leading to rapid photobleaching of smFISH spots or potentially incomplete cleavage of the fluorophores.

Notably, all buffers are subjected to ageing related to air exposure of the wash buffer and the readout probe cartridge buffer. When performing long measurements (>24h), it is recommended to change the buffers at least every 24h.

- Prime the fluidic system by running the following fluidic flow protocol: Flow 1 mL of 2xSSC buffer at 2 mL/min.Sequentially flow ~1 mL of solution at from each of the 24 wells of the readout probe cartridge.Flow ~1 mL of TCEP buffer.Flow ~1 mL of Wash buffer.Flow ~1 mL of Imaging buffer.Flow ~1 mL of 2x SSC buffer.

#### Imaging

#### Loading the sample

- Using the tweezers, transfer your sample onto a Kimwipe.

Keep hydrogel upwards. Be careful not to touch the hydrogel, especially the portion with the tissue.

- Using a razor blade gently trim the gel so that your sample fits the fluidic chamber gasket.

- Load your sample into the fluidic chamber.

Make sure that the fluidic chamber is perfectly clean. Any salt crystals or salt solution can corrode the chamber and compromise the correct MERFISH scope operation.

- In the fluidic system interface, launch the imaging buffer protocol: Flow ~ 1.5 mL of imaging buffer.

Note that this imaging buffer volume is designed for a fluidic chamber of about 2 cm × 1 cm × 1 mm. If using a larger fluidic chamber, the imaging volumes should be adjusted accordingly. The flow rate can also be adjusted.

- Using an alcohol pad, clean the bottom coverslip surface (remove any buffer solution in which the coverslip was immersed).

Make sure there are no marker residues or other contaminants on the surface. These can be dissolved by the objective oil, compromise the measurements and contaminate the objective.

- Load the fluidic chamber onto the microscope.

Before loading the fluidic chamber onto the microscope make sure the surface is clean and dry.

#### Starting the acquisition

- Start a complete MERFISH acquisition involving sequential rounds of imaging and hybridization, following the detailed recipe below: Capture fluorescent images of the selected FOVs.

Time depends on the number of FOVs, z-planes imaged and camera exposure time. Include a snapshot of the fluorescence fiducial beads deposited onto the surface. These beads serve as the fingerprint for each FOV and are crucial for re-registering the image stack during the decoding process.

- Launch a full hybridization round consisting of the following fluidic protocol: Cleavage protocol: Flow ~1.5 mL of cleavage buffer over 3 minutes.Flow another 0.15 mL of cleavage buffer over 15 minutes at a very low flow rate to complete the reaction.Flow ~1.5 mL of 2xSSC over 3 minutes to wash the cleavage buffer.Hybridization protocol: Flow ~1.5 mL of readout probes hybridization solution over 3 minutes.Flow another ~1.4 mL of readout probes hybridization solution over 14 minutes at low flow rate to complete the hybridization step.Flow ~0.75 mL of wash buffer over 1.5 minutes to remove the excess readout probe solution.Flow another ~0.5 mL of wash buffer solution over 5 minutes to complete the process.Imaging buffer protocol: Flow ~1.5 mL of imaging buffer over 3 minutes.

Note that the imaging buffer volumes and flow rates are optimized for a specific fluidic chamber (Bioptech, Focht Chamber System 2 [FCS2] equipped with a 1 mm thick rectangular gasket [F18524]).

- At the end of the run, remove the coverslip, and wash the entire system with plenty of nuclease-free water before the following run.

### Basic Protocol 5

#### Protocol title: Image decoding

This protocol outlines the steps for analyzing a MERFISH dataset using an existing pipeline (Moffitt et al., 2018; Moffitt, Hao, Wang, et al., 2016), including guidance on proper pipeline installation. The pipeline processes raw TIFF stacks as input and outputs the positions and identities of RNA molecules across the images. The high-level workflow consists of three main steps. First, images acquired across all hybridization rounds are re-registered to correct for small shifts in stage position that occur during repetitive rounds of imaging. Next, a normalization algorithm compensates for differences in smFISH spot intensity between the two smFISH color channels and across hybridization rounds. Finally, a pixel-based soft-decoding routine assigns the fluorescence intensity vector formed for each pixel across all images to one of the binary barcodes in the library.

In greater detail, during the re-registration step, the fiducial bead patterns serve as a fingerprint to re-align all images corresponding to each FOV. The locations of the fiducial beads are first determined through fitting, and an affine transformation is applied to align bead images from the same FOV across all imaging rounds. Additionally, chromatic corrections are performed to align images captured by two different cameras specific to the Alexa750 and Cy5 channels. At this stage, a high-pass filter is applied to remove background noise, and fluorescence spots are tightened using the Lucy-Richardson deconvolution, followed by minor smoothing with a low-pass filter to account for modest movements of RNA spots between rounds.

To address variations in smFISH spot intensities between hybridization rounds and channels, an optimization routine is applied to 25 randomly selected FOV. For each image, the 90th percentile of pixel intensities was used to initialize the process. RNA molecules are then decoded, and the intensities of spots corresponding to the 'on bits' of each barcode are averaged. These averages enabled quantitative comparisons of 'on biť intensities across imaging rounds. If there are differences, then the imagine intensities have not been properly normalized. To correct such differences, the algorithm employs an iterative process that successively decodes RNAs, recalculates these ‘on bit’ intensities, and adjusts the scaling of images to address residual differences in ‘on bit’ intensity in order to progressively minimize the intensity discrepancies.

Following the optimization routine, all FOVs are decoded by matching the intensity vector of each pixel to the nearest binary barcode in the library using the Euclidean distance. Pixels with a distance exceeding that of a single-bit flip are discarded. Adjacent pixels matching the same barcode are merged and considered as a single molecule. Each z-plane in the z-stack is decoded independently. Finally, the decoded RNA molecules are further filtered based on their area (the number of pixels assigned to that RNA) and an overall brightness (calculated from the Euclidean norm of the normalized image intensities in those pixels) to remove residual noise. The results are exported to csv format for subsequent analysis.

- 10. The pipeline executes the following steps: 1) build the decoder, 2) preprocess the data (re-registration of the images), 3) optimize parameters (normalization routine), 4) decode RNA (pixel-based soft-decoding routine), 5) compute RNA metadata, 6) calculate output performance, and 7) export the metadata. Completing the pipeline requires approximately 17 hours with the hardware configurations described above. For reference, below are the required times for analysis of this example dataset on our Linux system: decoder construction: 5s.preprocess: 47722s.init scale factors: 16s.optimize: 4431s.decode: 6763s.rna_metadata: 1971s.performance: 131s.export: 92s.

Computing times may vary depending on available hardware resources and dataset characteristics, such as the number of FOVs, z-stacks, and the length of binary barcodes in the library. Moreover, the pipeline is designed to run on both local machines, as shown in this tutorial, and high-performance computing platforms using a Slurm Workload Manager interface.

- 11. You can adjust the brightness and area thresholds applied to identified RNAs to better separate real RNAs from background, false-positive measurements. Ideal thresholds will vary between datasets.

Note that these thresholds are designed to distinguish spots associated with real mRNA from those resulting from noise and background. smFISH spots associated with noise are typically small in size with an area of 1 pixel (approximately 100 nm on our camera) and dim in brightness intensity. In contrast, smFISH spots associated with real RNA molecules are larger in size (at least 2 pixels in area) and significantly brighter than the background. After reviewing the area and brightness histograms in Figure 10 the threshold values can be adjusted in the script by editing the following lines:

- mDecoder.SetParameter('minimumBarcodeBrightness', 16);

- mDecoder.SetParameter('minimumBarcodeArea', 2);

- 12. Once decoding is complete, the initial MERFISH analysis results are saved in the Report folder, along with a barcode_metadata.csv file. This file includes details such as the x, y, and z coordinates of all decoded barcodes, among other information.

- 13. The pipeline generates several output analyses that are essential to review. These figures allow users to evaluate the overall quality of the dataset and, crucially, identify potential issues from the acquisition process that could affect the biological interpretation of the data. The geometric transformation summary (Figure 11) pertains to the initial step of the pipeline: the warping process. During this step, geometric transformations are applied to re-align images across all hybridization rounds, using fiducial beads as reference points. The appearance of patterns marked by unusually large offsets in the solid transforms (e.g., 200), scaling factors, or angle transformations may indicate issues during acquisition. Inspecting the raw .tiff images can help confirm such problems that are perhaps arising from hardware failures (e.g. motorized x-y stage).The optimization report plots (Figure 12) are particularly useful for evaluating the optimization process and identifying potential issues that may impact subsequent steps of the pipeline. Specifically, failure to compensate for variations in spot brightness across all hybridization rounds, as illustrated in the bit brightness panel, could indicate excessively bright spots in a specific hybridization round, the absence of bright spots in another round, or that the default number of optimization iterations (10 rounds) is insufficient. Additionally, reviewing the randomly selected raw .tiff files used in this routine may reveal further problems, such as the optimization being conducted on a FOV that does not contain any portion of the tissue.The area and brightness histograms (Figure 10) are invaluable for quickly assessing the quality of a dataset. Given the pixel-based nature of the decoding pipeline, a high-quality dataset typically exhibits a continuous distribution consisting of two distinct smFISH populations: one comprised of relatively dim and small spots representing noise and background, and another consisting of brighter, larger spots corresponding to signal as shown in this dataset. Greater separation between these populations facilitates the differentiation of spots associated with real mRNA from noise, a key hallmark of a high-quality dataset. However, issues inherent to the sample—such as poor RNA integrity, extensive autofluorescence, or suboptimal library design (e.g., the presence of highly abundant genes)—can reduce the separation between these populations, eventually rendering them indistinguishable. This narrowing complicates the selection of area and brightness thresholds, leading to suboptimal quality metrics.The plots in the error report file (Figure 13) are particularly valuable for assessing the decoded barcodes. Typically, most decoded barcodes correspond to mRNA species present in the library, with only a small proportion attributed to blank barcodes thus representing false positives. However, there are instances where one or more blank barcodes may appear among the most decoded barcodes. This phenomenon might originate from incredibly low detection efficiency or alternatively from barcode collision between two RNA species that often co-localize in space. Additionally, the error report is useful for detecting issues related to overcorrection of a bit, which is characterized by a threefold or greater increase in error rate for one or more bits. Such errors may arise for instance from problems related to the fluidic handling during the hybridization step.The FPKM correlation plot (Figure 14) provides a quantitative comparison between RNA species measured by MERFISH and those measured using an independent technique, such as bulk RNA-seq. Typically, this figure exhibits a 'hockey stick' shape: RNA species with abundances above 0.1–1 FPKM generally show a linear correlation between the two techniques, while low-abundance species, which are more susceptible to noise in both methods, tend to display weaker correlations. Significant deviations from the linear trend above 1 FPKM often indicate suboptimal detection efficiency. Additionally, this figure facilitates the identification of relatively abundant RNA species that are entirely uncorrelated between the two methods, warranting further investigation and caution during downstream analyses.Visualizing the spatial distribution of all decoded species provides valuable insights. Evaluating RNA spatial patterns by leveraging known biological contexts, along with examining the distribution of blank barcodes, offers a qualitative yet effective approach to identifying artifacts. Such artifacts may arise from specific regions of the sample (e.g., autofluorescent areas, out of focus regions) affecting individual FOVs. Although these figures are not automatically provided by the pipeline, we recommend the user to use the python script named “plot_barcodes_space.py” to generate and inspect this output as shown in Figure 15. This script is provided in the Dryad repository described above.

It is important to note that while these figures do not explicitly identify the exact source of the problem, they are valuable in narrowing down potential causes. More importantly, they offer a quick means of flagging potential issues before advancing to downstream analyses, such as single-cell analysis, where some problems may be less apparent and could be confounded by biological variability.

### SUPPORT PROTOCOL 1

#### Support protocol title: Coverslip silanization

This protocol outlines the process for cleaning, silanizing, and storing coverslips used in MERFISH sample preparation (Basic Protocols 1 and 2). The coverslips are first cleaned to remove any contaminants and then coated with a silane layer containing an allyl moiety. During hydrogel polymerization, the surface-bound allyl groups react with the acrylamide moieties, effectively cross-linking and thus stabilizing the polyacrylamide gel to the glass coverslips.

#### Materials

40-mm diameter, #1.5 coverslips (Bioptechs 40-1313-03193)

37% Hydrochloric acid (Sigma, 258148–2.5-GL)

100% Methanol (VWR, BDH1135–4LG)

Chloroform (VWR, BDH1109–4LG)

Allyltrichlorosilane, 95% (Sigma, 1077778–5G)

Triethylamine (FisherScientific, T0886–100mL)

100% ethanol (VWR, TX89125170HU)

Wafer boats (Entergris A23–0215)

Glass dishes (Electron Microscopy Sciences 70312–31)

Glass beakers (1 L volume)

Nitrogen gas source (AirGas, NF200)

Coverslip container

3D printed storage container (https://github.com/MoffittLab/3DParts)

Drierite (FisherScientific, AC219085000)

Plastic container (VWR, 36318–858)

Tweezers (McMaster Carr, 5669A44)

Parafilm (Sigma, P7793)

Nuclease-free water

Chemical fume hood

#### Protocol steps with step annotations:

CAUTION: All work detailed in this protocol should be conducted in a fume hood with the exception of the alcohol washing step and the nitrogen drying step, which can be performed outside of a hood. All solutions used in this protocol including the HCl/methanol solution, the chloroform/silane solution as well as the chloroform and water used to wash coverslips should be disposed of via the proper methods. For disposal, it is helpful to use a funnel to transfer the waste from the glass dishes to the waste container. Pouring directly from the dish can result in spills and splashes.

CAUTION: Hydrochloric acid is corrosive and toxic. Perform all operations in a chemical fume hood and wear appropriate personal protective equipment.

CAUTION: Methanol is toxic and flammable. Perform all operations in a chemical fume hood and wear appropriate personal protective equipment.

CAUTION: Chloroform is toxic and cancerogenic. Perform all operations in a chemical fume hood and wear appropriate personal protective equipment.

CAUTION: Allyltrichlorosilane is corrosive and flammable. Perform all operations in a chemical fume hood and wear appropriate personal protective equipment.

CAUTION: Triethylamine is toxic, corrosive and flammable. Perform all operations in a chemical fume hood and wear appropriate personal protective equipment.

#### Clean coverslips

The aim of this step is to remove any contaminants and unwanted material from the surface of the coverslips prior to silanization. This step is often critical for removing debris that scatters light and generates unwanted fluorescence background.

- Load coverslips into wafer boat (Figure 16A). Ensure that single coverslips are in the individual slots of the boat.Load multiple boats if running multiple batches.

- In the chemical hood in a 1 L beaker mix the following: 300 mL methanol.300 mL 37% HCl.

CAUTION: This is an exothermic reaction. It’s important to slowly pour the HCl onto methanol as it prevents overheating and excess splashing.

- Place wafer boat in a glass dish and cover with the HCl/methanol solution (Figure 16 B & C).

- Incubate for 30 minutes at RT.

- Fill a second glass dish with nuclease-free water for rinsing and transfer the water boat to this dish. If nuclease-free water is unavailable, DI water will also work.

- Empty the dish of water and repeat the wash for a total of three times.

This work can be done outside the chemical hood but be careful not to tip the wafer boat as the coverslips will fall out.

- Fill a third dish with 100% ethanol and submerge the coverslips for a final rinse.

- Remove the wafer boat, place on a clean bench, and immediately dry with nitrogen or in a 60°C oven for 15 minutes.

Ensure that the oven is clean and free of dust. Before moving forward with the protocol, make sure that all liquid is removed from the coverslips, as any residual water can interfere with the subsequent silanization step.

If not immediately proceeding to the silanization step, cover the wafer boat and contained coverslips with foil to protect them from dust. Take care to lightly cover the wafer boat, coverslips may break if wrapped tightly. Remove any broken coverslips before proceeding to silanization.

#### Silanization

The aim of this step is to coat the coverslips with a silane layer that contains a reactive moiety that will be covalently incorporated into polyacrylamide films.

CAUTION: The silanization solutions should be prepared and the silanization process should be conducted in a fume hood.

- Make a silanization solution by adding to a 1 L beaker the following: 0.6 mL triethylamine.600 mL chloroform.1.2 mL allyltrichlorosilane.

CAUTION: this step should produce a small amount of chlorine gas. Chlorine appears as a visible white gas on the surface and dissipates within a few minutes.

Before use, inspect the bottle of allyltrichlorosilane. If you observe precipitates, replace with a fresh bottle, as the presence or precipitate indicates polymerization of the silane inside the bottle.

- Ensure the solution is mixed by either swirling the liquid or using a stirrer (e.g. stirring rod or spatula).

It is recommended to use a glass spatula and avoid plastic, as it will dissolve.

- Transfer the coverslips in the wafer boat to a glass dish.

Mark the glass dish used for silanization and use only this dish for all silanization reactions. Do not mix dishes using them for other wash steps.

- Cover the coverslips with the silanization solution.

This solution can be safely used up to six times in the same session. Prolonged exposure to air leads to silane polymerization which is noticeable because of the formation of a thin white layer on top of the chloroform-silane solution.

- Cover the dish to prevent condensation of water with either a cap made of inert polymer such as polytetrafluoroethylene or by using parafilm.

If using parafilm, ensure that it never comes into contact with the solution as it will immediately dissolve and contaminate the surface of the coverslips.

- Incubate at RT for 30 minutes.

- While incubating, fill a second glass dish with 100% chloroform and a third glass dish with 100% ethanol. Both are going to be used to rinse the coverslips.

In this case, to prevent chloroform evaporation it is recommended to cover the dish with a cap made of inert polymer such as polytetrafluoroethylene.

- Rinse the coverslips by transferring the wafer boat from the chloroform-silane dish to the chloroform dish first, followed by submerging it into the ethanol dish.

- Take the wafer boat outside the chemical hood and dry it either with a nitrogen flow or, as an alternative, in an oven at 60°C for 15 minutes.

Before moving forward with the storage, make sure that all liquid is removed from the coverslips, as any residual water can react and hydrolyze the silane layer.

#### Storing coverslips

The silane layer is susceptible to hydrolysis and, thus, coverslips must be stored desiccated. If stored in the dark in a desiccated environment at room temperature, we have found that they can last at least 6 months (or even longer) if the Drierite is still blue. The quality of the silane layer can be tested by casting a poly-acrylamide gel as described in the Embedding and Clearing section of the MERFISH fixed-frozen protocol described above.

- Using a pair of tweezers, transfer coverslips to a 3D-printed storage container (Figure 16D).

- To minimize air exposure, wrap the 3D-printed storage container with parafilm around.

- In the plastic container, add Drierite to the bottom on the container to create small desiccator.

Drierite should be blue. If red or purple then water has been absorbed, and it should be replaced.

- Place coverslip container on top of the Drierite layer and close larger plastic container (Figure 16E).

- Seal the plastic container with parafilm.

- Store in dark for several weeks or until needed.

#### Support protocol title: Trolox Quinone Stock preparation

#### Introductory paragraph:

Immunofluorescent stains are useful for boundary labeling and cell segmentation especially for dense cell tissue like gut. Here, we describe the steps to label cell boundaries with antibodies in a MERFISH-compatible way. In short, oligo-labeled antibodies that possess single stranded DNA MERFISH readout sequences are incubated with the sample in 30% formamide to achieve boundary staining. Including oligo-labeled antibodies in your MERFISH sample is seamless and can be added to Basic Protocols 2 for fresh frozen samples. We elect to perform primary and secondary antibody staining in the hybridization buffer because the formamide content in the hybridization buffer effectively inhibits nucleases that could be present in the antibodies. Note that incubating antibodies in the MERFISH hybridization buffer might not work well for all antibody combinations, and antibody staining in this way should be tested on a case-by-case basis.

#### Primary antibody hybridization

The goal of this step is to co-stain your sample with the primary antibody against the cell boundary.

Note that antibody staining can be performed simultaneously with encoding probe staining by combining the mixtures in the same hybridization buffer master mix.

- Prepare hybridization chamber: Add a layer of parafilm to the bottom of a large Petri dish and gently press down with a cap from a 50 mL tube to ensure the parafilm adheres to the surface.

- Combine the appropriate volume of your primary antibody with hybridization buffer to a final volume of 50 μL of staining solution in hybridization buffer for each sample as prepared in Basic Protocol 2. For details on the preparation of hybridization buffer, please refer to Supporting Protocol 3.

The concentration of the primary antibody depends on the antibody itself. For instance, for Na-K ATPase antibodies (Abcam, ab76020) the optimal final concentration is approximately 3 μg/mL.

Notably, the combined volume of anchoring and antibody solution should be approximately 10% of the total staining solution volume (e.g., no more than 5 μL for a 50 μL staining solution). Diluting the formamide concentration in the hybridization buffer might negatively impact the oligo hybridization and lead to higher background signals.

- Aspirate the pre-hybridization wash mixture from each sample and, using the tweezers, move the coverslip into the large Petri dish (the tissue is facing up).

Before pipetting the hybridization solution, it’s important to make sure you aspirate the excess formamide from the sample using the aspirator before you pipette the hybridization mixture. Leftover wash buffer might dilute the concentration of our hybridization mixture.

- Add one droplet of 50 μL of hybridization mixture in directly on top of the tissue slices.

The goal here is to completely cover the tissue slices with solution; thus, adjust the hybridization volume accordingly. For instance, larger tissues such as intestinal strips or Swiss rolls may require > 100 μL of hybridization mixture per sample.

- Place a wet Kimwipe soaked with nuclease-free water inside the hybridization chamber. This will help to saturate the humidity inside the chamber and avoid evaporation of the solution thus changes in its concentration.

The oven is humidified as an extra precaution against the evaporation of the hybridization solution.

As an alternative to the Kimwipe, the humidity of the hybridization chamber can also be maintained by sealing it with parafilm. However, care must be taken while wrapping the parafilm as not to perturb the drop of hybridization solution on the coverslip.

- Place the lid back on top of the Petri dish.

- Place the Petri dish in a 37°C hybridization oven that is humidified and incubate for 24 hours.

Make sure the outside of the Petri dish is clean before placing it in the incubator otherwise use a Kimwipe and 70% ethanol to clean it.

- Proceed to the post-hybridization wash step in Basic Protocols 2.

- Aspirate the wash solution and add 3 mL of fresh post-hybridization wash solution and incubate for 30 minutes at 47°C.

- Aspirate the wash solution, add 3 mL of post-hybridization wash and immediately proceed to the secondary antibody staining step.

#### Staining with the oligo-labeled-secondary antibody

The oligo-labeled-secondary antibody possesses a single stranded oligonucleotide that is the reverse complement of a MERFISH readout probe. The oligo is incorporated into the polyacrylamide gel and thus preserves the coordinates of the cell boundary.

- Prepare hybridization chamber. Add a layer of parafilm to the bottom of a large Petri dish and gently press down with a cap from a 50 mL tube to ensure the parafilm adheres to the surface.

- Prepare 50 μL of secondary antibody staining solution per sample in hybridization buffer. Add 10 μL of your diluted oligo-labeled secondary antibody to 40 μL of hybridization buffer. Pipette up and down 25 times to mix.

The concentration of the oligo-labeled secondary antibody should be independently determined for your tissue type.

- Aspirate the post-hybridization wash mixture from each sample and, using the tweezer, move the coverslip into the large Petri dish (the tissue is facing up).

- Add one droplet of 50 μL of hybridization mixture in directly on top of the tissue slices.

Adjust the volume to the tissue size. Larger tissues sections may require >100 μL of hybridization mixture per sample.

- Place a wet Kimwipe with nuclease-free water inside the hybridization chamber. This will help to saturate the humidity inside the chamber and avoid evaporation of the solution thus changes in its concentration.

- Place the lid back on top of the Petri dish.

- Cover the dish with aluminum foil.

- Place the Petri dish in a 37°C hybridization oven that is humidified and incubate for 24 hours

- Continue with “Embedding sample into a hydrogel” in Basic Protocol 2 and proceed to imaging.

## COMMENTARY:

### Critical Parameters:

One of the most critical factors is maintaining an RNase-free environment and using RNase-free chemicals and tools. This is accomplished by designating specific benches for RNA work and using RNase decontamination solutions to keep the workspace and equipment clean. If needed, solutions and reagents such as antibodies can be tested for RNase contamination using commercial kits (e.g., RNaseAlert™ Lab Test Kit, ThermoFisher Scientific, AM1964). Ensuring high RNA quality within the tissue is equally important. Before starting any protocol, it is highly recommended to assess RNA integrity using the RNA integrity number (RIN) or DV200, with commercially available assays such as the Bioanalyzer (Agilent). These assays, which can be performed immediately after tissue harvesting or cryosectioning, are invaluable for detecting RNA degradation, which leads to less and dimmer single molecules spots and ultimately lower detection efficiency of target genes. For mouse intestine samples, a RIN of 9 or above is expected.

### Troubleshooting Table:

Multiple common issues can arise in the execution of these protocols that can lead to poor- or low-quality measurements. These are summarized in Table 2.

#### Understanding Results

Executing the MERFISH pipeline relies on three key components: proper preparation of the gut tissue (Basic Protocol 1 and Basic Protocol 2), successful library amplification (Basic Protocol 3), and accurate sample imaging and analysis (Basic Protocol 4 and Basic Protocol 5). At the microscope, samples processed according to this pipeline display high signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) smFISH spots across all tissue regions, with minimal autofluorescence and background signals (Figure 18). The most critical aspect of sample preparation is preserving RNA integrity, particularly during tissue harvesting. Failure to do so leads to sparse smFISH spots with a lower SNR (Figures 18A & B). A modest SNR degradation may occur when imaging extends beyond 36 hours, typically affecting later rounds. This is associated with a decline in imaging buffer performance, which can be mitigated by replacing the imaging reagents every 24–36 hours. Benchmarking and inspecting the spatial distribution of specific genes is also a useful metric to understand and validate the results.

High SNR smFISH spots in the first round of readout probe staining is often a very faithful reporter of the quality of a full MERFISH measurement on that sample. Once all imaging rounds have been collected, the image data can be used to identify and decode RNAs using an existing pipeline (github.com/ZhuangLab/MERFISH_analysis)—detailed in the Basic Protocol 5. The spatial distribution of the identified RNAs as well as internal blank barcode controls—barcodes not assigned to an RNA which serve as direct measures of false positive rates—are also useful metrics of the quality of the sample preparation. An example of a decoded dataset is shown in Figure 15, displaying the spatial distribution of eight genes from a library of approximately 1000 genes across all layers of a cross-section of the mouse colon. Open-access mouse datasets are available for both fresh-frozen (Petukhov et al., 2022) and fixed-frozen approaches (Cadinu et al., 2024).

Both the final and intermediate products of the encoding probes amplification process—template amplification via qPCR, in vitro transcription, and reverse transcription—should always undergo quality control using denaturing polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis. The bands from each step should show progressively shorter lengths (Figure 9). During in vitro transcription, the reverse primer is removed, making the RNA products shorter. Similarly, after reverse transcription, the forward primers equipped with 3' RNA nucleobases are removed during the alkaline hydrolysis step. While the length of the products is important, the amount of final DNA encoding probes is equally critical for assessing the results. Although the efficiency of qPCR and in vitro transcription is generally high, reverse transcription is less efficient. Depending on the library and the amount of input RNA per reaction, the fraction of RNA probes converted into DNA encoding probes should typically range between 20% and 30%.

# In situ profiling of plasma cell clonality with image-based single-cell transcriptomics

**Authors:** Evan Yang; Jose Aceves-Salvador; Carlos Castrillon; Uli S Herrmann; Elliot H Akama-Garren; Michael C Carroll; Jeffrey R Moffitt

**Affiliations:** 1 Program in Cellular and Molecular Medicine, Boston Children’s Hospital, Boston, MA 02115, USA | 2 Department of Microbiology, Blavatnik Institute, Harvard Medical School, Boston, MA 02115, USA | 3 Broad Institute of Harvard and MIT, Cambridge, MA 02142, USA.

## Abstract

Image-based single-cell transcriptomics can identify diverse cell types within intact tissues. However, in adaptive immunity, V(D)J recombination generates unique immune receptors within cells of the same type, leading to important functional variation that is not yet defined by these methods. Here we introduce B-cell-receptor multiplexed error robust fluorescence in situ hybridization (BCR-MERFISH), which distinguishes plasma cell clones based on V-gene usage in combination with transcriptome profiling. We demonstrate that BCR-MERFISH accurately identifies V-gene usage in cell culture and in mice with restricted or native plasma cell diversity. We then use BCR-MERFISH to reveal the microbiota-dependent changes in plasma cell abundance, clonal diversity, and public clonotype usage in the mouse gut and the non-uniform distribution of plasma cell clones along the mouse ileum. As tissue context is an essential modulator of plasma cell dynamics, we anticipate that BCR-MERFISH may offer new insights into a wide range of immunological questions.

## Main

B and T cells have the remarkable ability to identify a range of pathogens and antigens due to the sequence diversity of their associated immune receptors1,2. B cells generate this massive sequence variation in their B-cell receptors (BCR) through V(D)J recombination and somatic hypermutation3–6, and, as B cells differentiate into plasma B cells, this diversity is carried over into the secreted antibody repertoire. B cells that carry highly similar BCR sequences are considered clones, and changes in B cell clonality within a tissue are indicative of B cell immune responses7–9. Sequencing-based methods such as bulk or single-cell BCR-seq have proven adept at characterizing changes in clonality and have been used to link high clonal diversity to proper immune surveillance and tissue homeostasis, or low clonal diversity to infection10–12, autoimmunity12–14, and cancer15.

While the B cell response can act systemically through circulating antibody-secreting plasma B cells, many B cell behaviors are inherently local and involve specific cellular interactions in different tissue contexts. For example, within germinal centers local interactions between T follicular helper cells, follicular dendritic cells, and unique germinal center B cell clones regulate the selection and clonal expansion of specific clones16–18. Similarly, local interactions are also important in disease. For instance, aberrant interactions between B cells and T follicular helper or dendritic cells has been implicated in the breakage of immune tolerance and the production of autoantibodies16,19–21. More broadly, atypical accumulation of B cells in specific tissues or tissue sites has been associated with diseases such as ulcerative colitis22, B cell cancers23,24, and systemic lupus erythematosus13,25.

The importance of cellular interactions and tissue context in these B cell functions has led to the introduction of technologies that can provide spatially resolved measurements of B cell clonality. For example, Confetti mice discriminate B cell clones through one of ten different genetically encoded two-fluorophore combinations and have been used to reveal the evolution of germinal center (GC) B cells towards pauciclonality within autoreactive GC of the spleen25 or in Peyer’s Patches (PP) following oral immunization26. Yet as a genetically encoded fluorescent measure of clonality, Confetti provides no direct link to sequence features of the BCR, provides limited information on the cellular identity and behavior of surrounding cells, and is restricted to genetically modified organisms. Recently spatial transcriptomic methods have been extended to characterize features of the adaptive immune system. Spatial V(D)J27, SPTCR-seq28, Stereo-XCR-seq29, and Slide-TCR-Seq30 leverage spatial capture arrays to characterize both transcriptome expression and sequence features of the BCR27,29 or the T cell receptor (TCR)28,29 and, thus, reveal the structure of tissues via gene expression, provide an estimate of local cellular content, and define local measures of B-cell or T-cell clonality. However, the resolution of these methods is multi-cellular, either due to physical limits on capture resolution (10 to 50 microns27,28,30) or the need to spatially aggregate sparse RNA measurements29; thus, these methods have only reported an inference of the local environment around immune cells or of the single-cell linkage of heavy and light chains27–30. For these reasons, there remains a need for spatially resolved methods that can directly characterize sequence features of immune receptors while simultaneously profiling gene expression, both at single-cell resolution.

Here, we present BCR-MERFISH (B Cell Receptor Multiplexed Error-Robust Fluorescence In Situ Hybridization), a single-cell spatial method that simultaneously measures plasma B cell clonality and the transcriptome of their surrounding tissues (Fig. 1a). BCR-MERFISH is built on MERFISH31,32, which leverages successive rounds of fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) to create optical barcodes that distinguish hundreds to thousands of unique RNA molecules with sub-cellular resolution within intact tissue samples31–36. In BCR-MERFISH, B cell clones are identified via optical barcodes that reveal the unique combination of heavy and light chain V gene usage as well as the heavy chain constant region. To overcome sequence homology between V regions, we introduce homology-aware probe design and barcoding schemes that leverage the highly expressed BCR mRNA in plasma cells. We demonstrate accurate V gene identification in cell culture, in mice with a restricted BCR repertoire, and by comparing to BCR-seq of wild type mice. To demonstrate the biological potential of BCR-MERFISH, we chart the abundance, location, and clonality of plasma cells in the gut of specific pathogen free (SPF) or germ-free (GF) mice. These measurements demonstrate the role that the microbiome plays in plasma cell abundance and clonal diversity, confirms that public clonotypes seen in GC B cells are represented in plasma cell populations, and discover that plasma cells are not uniformly distributed even along short lengths of the small intestine. With the ability to simultaneously define plasma cell clonality based on sequence features of the BCR and map cell types and states in the surrounding tissue, we anticipate that BCR-MERFISH may prove to be a useful tool for profiling interactions with and effects of elements of the adaptive immune system in a wide range of tissue contexts.

## Results

### Identifying B cell clones with homology-aware probe design and encoding

The central challenge to identifying B cell clones via the sequence of the BCR with FISH-based methods is the high degree of sequence homology within the gene segments that comprise the heavy and light chains of the BCR. During B cell maturation, the primary sequence of the heavy and light chain of the BCR is created through V(D)J recombination5,7,37. The many tens of germline V, D, or J gene segments from which this process selects arose through genetic duplication38 and therefore share high degrees of sequence homology. Unfortunately, homologous genes are challenging for FISH-based detection, as hybridization permits some sequence mismatch; thus, probes designed for one RNA target may bind several off-target RNAs with sufficient homology. Standard FISH-probe design approaches identify and discard such probes32; however, for sets of genes with substantial degrees of homology, these design approaches may produce no viable probes for many targets.

Here we address this limitation by introducing two complementary approaches. First, we developed a homology-aware FISH-probe design algorithm (Methods). The key insight to this approach is that sets of homologous genes can be organized via their relative similarity and that homology between gene subsets can be managed by targeting groups of highly similar RNAs, rather than individual RNAs (Fig. 1b). Specifically, we developed an iterative algorithm that leverages a similarity-tree-based representation of relative homology to guide probe design. In this approach, standard probe design methods32 are used to identify all target RNAs with sufficient dissimilarity from all other targets to support a desired number of unique probes per RNA. Any RNA that does not support sufficient probe numbers—because of its high degree of homology to other RNA—is then grouped with the nearest RNA or set of RNAs, as determined by the similarity tree. Probe design is then repeated with the critical difference that potential homology to other RNAs is only considered for RNAs outside of a group and potential probes are not penalized for homology to RNAs within a group. This process then iterates until enough probes have been designed for all RNAs or groups of RNAs (Fig. 1b).

We used this homology-aware probe-design approach to group all 188 IGHV (VH) genes and 102 IGKV/IGLV (VKVL) into 80 VH and 68 VKVL targetable groups (Fig. S1a–d, Table S1, Methods). We did not use this approach to design probes against the D or J segments due to their shorter length. Despite their high degrees of homology, 67 of the 188 VH genes were directly targetable with the remaining genes organized into 13 groups of various sizes (Fig. S1a,b; Table S1). Similarly, 63 of the 102 VKVL genes were directly targetable with the remaining genes organized into 5 groups (Fig. S1c,d; Table S1). Supporting our analysis, our similarity trees reproduced the established family organization for both the heavy and light V genes (Fig. S1a,c) and all members of each of the V gene groups produced by our algorithm were drawn from the same families (Fig. S1a–d; Table S1). For genes that could be detected without grouping, we chose to label them by their gene name (e.g., IGHV1–47) whereas grouped genes were named via the gene family that comprised that group followed by a unique letter (e.g., IGHV1-A or IGHV1-B; Table S1).

Despite this grouping of high homology genes, we reasoned that some degree of off-target binding between groups may still occur due, perhaps, to residual homology or sequence modification by somatic hyper mutation. Thus, we also created a homology-resistant encoding scheme (Fig. 1c–e). In this approach, targetable genes or groups are assigned a unique binary barcode with a fixed Hamming weight (HW), i.e., the number of bits with a value of ‘1’ (Fig. 1c). All RNAs that are bound by only probes targeted to that RNA would generate a barcode with that fixed HW (Fig. 1d). By contrast, if an RNA had bound probes from multiple targets, due to residual homology between the two, it would generate a signal that represents the combination of both barcodes—an event we call a collision—which would be clearly detected by a larger observed HW (Fig. 1d). Such approaches have been used previously with MERFISH to identify and discard error containing barcodes31; however, as collisions are driven by the sequences of the V genes, in this case, collision barcodes are likely V gene specific and, thus, could still be used to distinguish B cell clones (Fig. 1e). However, as it is not possible to uniquely determine the barcodes that collided because such barcodes cannot be associated with unique V gene groups; thus, we label these unique collision events separately (i.e., Collision 1; Fig. 1d,e; Methods; Table S1).

Leveraging these approaches, we generated a set of MERFISH encoding probes that collectively define the different VH and VKVL groups. VH and VKVL genes are decoded by separate 14-bit barcodes, each associated with an orthogonal set of readout probes to allow their combined measurements (Tables S1&S2; Fig. S1e–j). In addition, as B cells also undergo class switch recombination39 to select a specific constant region of the heavy chain (Fc), we also generated probes against the 7 different Fc regions (IgD, IgM, IgA, IgE, IgG1, IgG2, and IgG3; Tables S2, S3, &S4). Collectively, these probes should be able to distinguish between 80×68=5440 clones defined by their unique VH/VKVL pairs. Additionally, with the 7 different Fc regions, we can distinguish 5440×7=38,080 different possible B cells (Fig. S1e–j). Nonetheless, it is important to note that this definition of clonality differs from that used by sequencing-based methods, which typically includes both the selection of V, D, and J region as well as some degree of homology (often 90%) in the sequence of the complement determining region 3 (CDR3)40. Finally, due to unique readout probes being associated with each bit, these measurements can be performed in combination with standard MERFISH, allowing plasma cell clonality tracking to be layered upon standard MERFISH measurements (Fig. 1a). Collectively, we term this approach BCR-MERFISH.

### BCR-MERFISH accurately identifies VH and VKVL gene groups in single cells

To test the accuracy of V gene labeling with our homology-aware and -resistant probes, we created high expression plasmids containing a variety of distinct VH genes in combination with a defined D and J, driven by the constitutively active Cytomegalovirus (CMV) promoter (Fig. 1f; Methods). We then transfected HEK293 cells with a set of plasmids containing a known subset of VH genes and imaged them with BCR-MERFISH using probes targeting only the VH genes (Methods). As expected, individual cells showed bright fluorescent signals that varied in their on-off pattern of fluorescence across the multiple rounds of imaging, with all transfected cells showing the same pattern when a single construct was used and different cells showing different patterns when a complex collection of plasmids were used (Fig. S2a,b; Fig. 1f).

To quantify the patterns of observed fluorescence, we integrated the fluorescence within individual cells and normalized the intensities across imaging rounds (Fig. 1g; Fig. S2c). In samples containing multiple different VH genes, we observed a diversity of optical patterns that were statistically distinguishable (Fig. 1h), were reproduced across replicate measurements (Fig. 1i), and showed limited numbers of patterns that failed our collision detection (Fig. 1j). Importantly, essentially all patterns that passed the collision detection could be matched to barcodes associated with individual VH groups (Fig. 1g,h; Methods), cells assigned to the same VH group showed highly consistent optical barcodes (Fig. S2d), and VH groups that contained more V genes, such as IGHV1-G, were observed more frequently than V gene groups associated with a single V gene (Fig. 1h,k; Fig. S2d). Collectively, these observations support the ability of BCR-MERFISH to distinguish VH gene groups.

To quantify the accuracy of BCR-MERFISH, we compared the identified VH gene groups to the subset of V genes included in these measurements. 87% of VH genes included in our plasmid set were detected with BCR-MERFISH in at least one cell, while 89% of transfected cells were matched to a V gene included in the set (Fig. 1k,l), supporting the accuracy of BCR-MERFISH. Moreover, of the distinguishable optical patterns we observed, only 7% were detected as collision events, suggesting both that our probe design strategy was effective at managing the high-degree of homology between V genes and that our collision-detection scheme could identify these cases. Finally, we included in our barcode set valid barcodes that were not assigned to individual V genes and for which no encoding probes were created. These ‘Blank’ barcodes serve as an internal measure of our false positive rate (Table S1). Only 0.3% of cells were associated with a Blank barcode, providing additional support for the accuracy of our V gene calling with BCR-MERFISH.

We performed similar measurements with the VKVL genes and observed a similar accuracy in our ability to define VKVL with BCR-MERFISH (Fig. S2e–h). Taken together, these experiments support the ability of BCR-MERFISH to both distinguish distinct heavy and light chain V gene groups with optical barcodes and, in the vast majority of cases, associate these unique barcodes with the identity of the V gene group.

### BCR-MERFISH accurately identifies V gene groups in mice

In order to validate the ability of BCR-MERFISH to identify V gene groups in situ, we first turned to a transgenic mouse that harbors a knock-in of a prearranged BCR (564Igi; C57BL/6)25,41,42. As this mouse is RAG-proficient and contains an unarranged BCR locus, we anticipate some diversity in V gene usage. Nonetheless, we expect a strong enrichment of plasma cells using the prearranged heavy and light chain V gene pair (564H: IGHV1–53, 564K: IGKV4–59; Fig. 2a)25,41,42. To determine whether BCR-MERFISH observed this enrichment, we harvested a tissue rich in plasma cells—the ileum—from 8-week-old 564Igi mice and imaged sections of this tissue with BCR-MERFISH (Fig. 2b; Methods). As expected, we observed IgA+ plasma cells in the lamina propria (LP) of these ileal slices (Fig. 2b). Importantly, BCR-MERFISH identified the expected limited diversity of VH and VKVL gene groups within these plasma cells (Fig. S2i,j): 53% of plasma cells were associated with 564H and 96% with 564K. Moreover, we generated single-molecule FISH probes (Table S2) targeting only the 564H and 564K V genes and found that they further supported the presence of IgA+/564K+ ileal plasma cells that do not use the 564H V gene (Fig. S2k). Collectively, these measurements support the in situ accuracy of BCR-MERFISH.
